author: WoMin
title: Press Release | African Women Leading the Fight for Climate Justice
content:
From 5–8 October 2026, Yaoundé, Cameroon, will host the fourth regional

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA) under the theme

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations

! The landmark gathering unites women across West and Central Africa to strengthen their fight for climate justice rooted in ecofeminist resistance and the defence of the commons—land, forests, water, seeds and other resources collectively sustained and stewarded by communities. While Africa’s contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions remains minimal, its communities—particularly women in rural, coastal, and forest areas—face disproportionate climate impacts. The WCA highlights this fundamental injustice and the climate debt owed by historically polluting nations and multinationals to the continent.


The overall objective of the Women’s Climate Assembly is to strengthen and unify a Pan African ecofeminist movement for climate justice that connects women’s collective struggles. Key objectives include women’s leadership, fostering shared strategies for climate justice, promoting community-based alternatives centred on food sovereignty and sustainable resource management, and advancing calls for climate reparations and just development models.


Climate reparations – more than empty promises


African women, who play vital roles in food production, water management and protecting natural resources, are on the front lines of a deepening climate crisis, defending their lands and livelihoods against land degradation, droughts, extreme weather and the expansion of extractive industries such as oil and gas, alongside conflicts over resources and critical minerals. The scale of this injustice is stark: the World Meteorological Organisation’s latest

State of the Climate in Africa 2025

 reports that climate- and weather-related hazards affected at least 13 million people and caused more than 3,000 reported deaths across Africa in 2025 alone, with floods, droughts and tropical cyclones devastating communities across the continent. Rising temperatures, ocean warming and accelerating sea-level rise are further undermining food systems, livelihoods and ecosystems. Yet Africa has contributed the least to the climate crisis while bearing a disproportionate share of its impacts.


These losses cannot be treated as an unavoidable cost of development or left for African communities to finance. This year’s WCA theme makes a powerful call for climate reparations that go beyond empty promises of future aid, demanding substantial, consistent resources for loss and damage, adaptation, ecosystem restoration and community-led alternatives, alongside accountability by those most responsible for historical and ongoing emissions.


Co-hosted by Green Development Advocates, WoMin African Alliance and other partners, the Assembly will bring together over 75 women community leaders and activists, NGOs and allies from Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, DRC, Guinea Conakry, Liberia, Nigeria, Sierra Leone and Senegal. By uniting women’s struggles against exploitative industries and false climate solutions, the WCA embodies a vital ecofeminist resistance essential for the future of Africa and the planet. It offers a collective call to action for climate justice rooted in solidarity, sovereignty, reparations, and sustainable alternatives.


“The Women’s Climate Assembly taking place in Cameroon will allow women from other countries to experience firsthand the realities of Cameroonian women’s lives impacted by major projects and how they overcome these challenges.” –


Bela Marie Victorine, Cameroon


A permanent platform for African women-led resistance


Building on previous assemblies held in

Nigeria

 and

Senegal

, the space serves as a powerful political platform where community women on the front line share their struggles, build solidarity, and develop ecofeminist analyses rooted in their lived realities. The 2026 edition aims to transform the WCA into a permanent platform spanning local, national, subregional, and Pan African levels to amplify women’s voices and demands which are often missed in national and global discourse.


The WCA continues to be a pivotal space for strategy building, learning, organising, solidarity, and movement-building. Key sessions include discussions on national and sub-regional assembly processes; climate crisis impacts in Africa and strategies for resistance and alternatives led by women. Thematic …

author: Frashia Muthoni Karanja
title: The Red Earth Between Us
content:
Before steel crossed Kimuka, morning arrived on bare soles pressing into the earth, you could hear the footsteps before you saw the people. The striking red volcanic soil, rich in iron oxides, would easily stick and cake sandals when wet. The visible stains on livestock, rusty-red taint would easily contrast with the green and dry-yellow grass of Kajiado plains. By evening it had climbed into socks, fingernails, cooking pots and mattresses.


Women woke first. Muthoni was up by the time roosters crowed. The cold had unsettled sleep, her mother was crouched beside the hearth, blowing gently into last night’s charcoal until the first orange glow returned. Smoke thickened beneath the low roof, stinging Muthoni’s eyes. Then the shifting would begin from the

bomas,

 hooves scrapping, goats jostling inside a thorned fence. Across the ridge another woman was sweeping her compound with a twig broom. Her body was already answering an inherited clock that did not care for alarms. 


She tied her

leso

, its fabric softened by years of washing, and stepped outside. The air smelled of smoke from last night’s fires, of damp grass, of goats shifting in their sleep. Somewhere, a rooster misjudged the hour. She balanced the yellow jerrycan on her hip and began the walk toward the borehole, joining other women. They greeted each other softly, voices low, conserving breath for the climb back.


“How is your mother?”


“Still coughing.”


“And the calves?”


“Two survived.”


 These talks were an inventory of the bodies, of loss, of endurance.


The land around Kimuka was neither spectacular nor gentle, it was useful. It fed goats and cattle, held maize when the rains were kind, punished when they were not. Nobody remembered making these paths. They wandered between grazing fields and boreholes, around anthills and stubborn acacia. Children widened them on their way to school, chasing one another across the plains with duty shoes and tucked uniforms. By the time bicycles found them, they already knew their destinations.


Muthoni could tell of an afternoon storm before the first cloud gathered. She watched the termites instead, two or three days before heavy rains, the anthills opened new breathing holes and winged termites gathered just beneath the crust, waiting. Earth always inhaled before it drank. If the swallows flew low enough to skim the grass and the weaver birds abandoned the acacias for thicker thorn trees, she knew to bring in the washing before noon. Clouds have their language too, the harmless ones drifted high, white and lazy above the Ngong Hills. The dangerous ones arrived with the wind from Ndeiya in uneven layers, their bellies dark as wet cowhide, carrying the smell of rain before they carried the rain itself. Her mother had taught her that land listened.


“When you speak badly of it,” her mother used to say, “it will refuse you.”


So Muthoni spoke kindly, even when the soil cracked beneath her feet during dry seasons, even when crops failed, and hunger thinned the air inside the house. She thanked the ground before planting. She whispered apologies when she spilled hot water into the dirt.


Kimuka was not untouched by the world beyond it. Kameme FM, Radio Jambo and Classic FM carried voices from Nairobi, from further still, and entertainment with an array of music variety. The big Kenya Bus services never came this far, they stopped at Ngong where the tarmac ended. Kimuka belonged to battered Peugeot station wagons, feet and bicycles. Young men left and returned wearing different accents, different trousers. But change came slowly, like erosion noticeable only when you pause long enough to compare before and after.


Until the men in yellow helmets arrived.


They came first as rumours.


“They say a big road is coming.”


“Not a road.”


“A train.”


“How can a train come here?”


Then as paper, maps unrolled on makeshift tables under trees. Lines drawn with a confidence that did not ask permission. The first time Muthoni saw them, she was returning from the market, a sack of maize flour balanced on her back. A cloud of dust rose ahead of her, thick and unfamiliar. She slowed, her heart lifting into her throat, not fear exactly, but alertness.


The men moved differently, their steps were decisive and clipped. They had boots that pressed the soil flat. They wore helmets the colour of ripe mangoes, and vests bright enough to wound the eye. Their voices cut through the air in sharp syllables that rose and …

author: Ayoola Babalola
title: Too big to regulate
content:
In September 2024, Nigeria achieved something it had been promised for decades: the Dangote Petroleum Refinery began producing petrol on Nigerian soil. At 650,000 barrels per day,

the largest single-train refinery on earth

, it was a genuine industrial landmark.

Yet, by early 2026, Nigerian consumers were paying petrol prices roughly 12 percent above what competitive imports would have cost, according to a shelved

World Bank report

.

It is well argued by

scholars

 that Nigerian merchant capital did not emerge organically from agricultural surpluses or small manufacturing. It was shaped, from the colonial era onward, by three distinctive features: import-substitution policies that protected specific domestic interests; an oil economy that concentrated state revenues in few hands; and a “political settlement,” in the words of economist and professor Mushtaq Khan, that tied business access to political proximity rather than competitive performance.

The

Dantata

 family were among the trading families of northern Nigeria, enriched under colonial commodity boards that set paltry prices paid to farmers for export crops, with the boards accumulating surpluses that sometimes exceeded 100 percent of expected earnings. Licensed Buying Agents extracted their own share between the farmgate and export terminal. Farmers received the smallest portion of the value their labor produced. Aliko Dangote, Dantata’s great-grandson, is the chairman of Dangote Industries Ltd.

Nigeria’s “backward integration policy,” launched in 2002 to develop domestic manufacturing through tariff protection and tax incentives, was sound in principle. In practice, the political settlement governing it systematically concentrated its benefits in conglomerates with pre-existing political access. Nigeria’s industrial policy became a form of legislated primitive accumulation where the state manufactured the conditions for monopoly capital to form, and connected families captured those conditions first.

Nigeria’s cement capacity grew from roughly 2 million to nearly 48 million metric tonnes per annum between 2002 and 2019. Dangote invested in massive-scale kilns that outcompeted rivals, developed coal-mining operations to cut fuel costs, negotiated machinery discounts from Chinese contractors, and maintained a cost-to-revenue ratio of 30 to 40 percent against Lafarge Nigeria’s 70 to 80 percent. By Schumpeterian standards, this was a genuine competitive success.

But between 2011 and 2016, Dangote Cement’s profits more than tripled, whereas average wages per employee, over the same period,

fell in real terms

. The effective corporate tax rate on Nigerian cement operations was approximately 2 percent in 2016, against a statutory 30 percent. This was achieved by continuously rolling “pioneer status” tax holidays across new production lines as previous exemption windows expired.

Between 2010 and 2017, Dangote Cement earned NGN 1.7 trillion in profits and paid NGN 90 billion in taxes: a realized rate of roughly 5 percent

.

The “paradox of costs” holds that while rising wages reduce individual firm margins, they increase aggregate demand and, ultimately, total profit rates across the economy. A monopolist that suppresses wages and minimizes its fiscal contribution may maximize its own returns while shrinking both the purchasing power its sales depend on and the state resources needed to sustain it. When commodity prices fell in 2014, and Nigerian consumer spending contracted sharply, DIL’s food-processing businesses showed signs of this structural overcapacity: markets created by policy, but without the wage growth to sustain them.

Still, Dangote Refinery represents a qualitative leap in strategic importance. Its capacity reportedly

exceeds Nigeria’s entire domestic fuel demand

. Practically, it now supplies about 62 percent of Nigeria’s petrol, becoming the main supplier after import licenses were restricted. The monopoly emerged as failed state refineries and excluded modular operators left a technically superior but politically difficult private monopoly replacing a corrupt state one.

The “crude-for-naira” arrangement inaugurated in October 2024 is the analytical crux of the “fair deal” question. Despite its name, the scheme is not a simple currency substitution. It is not merely barter.

NNPC supplies crude to Dangote in naira; Dangote, in return, sells the refined equivalent of the received product to Nigerian market(ers) in naira

. Though …

author: Yassir Gadid
title: Türkiye’s Security Export: Why Africa’s New Air Force Costs Less Than a Fighter Jet’s Spare Parts
content:
Drones have become a primary mechanism of warfare on many fronts around the world. Those fronts range from the war between Russia and Ukraine to the conflict between the United States and Iran. Drones are used to achieve air superiority, a reconnaissance advantage, and highly precise strategic strikes along the front lines. Those strikes range from the pinpoint targeting of individual objectives to larger-scale strikes against strategic targets and infrastructure.


What makes drones a unique tool of warfare is that their low cost and ease of manufacture make them accessible to poorer nations as part of their military arsenals and more broadly to meet their needs for the modernization and development of their military industries. Türkiye has emerged as one of the leading countries in the international landscape of drone technology. The country has a history of drone manufacturing dating back to the 1990s through the drone trial using the UAV-X1 projects at the time. The technical breakthrough happened in the 2010s. An example is the Bayraktar TB2 drone system (three drones plus a ground unit) that was widely used in the war in Ukraine and which made its maiden flight in 2014.


An interesting topic of analysis is Türkiye’s role in transforming the military industries of African nations and in lowering the cost of air superiority. That enabled African states to have strike capabilities without relying on expensive fighter jets deals. This contributes to changing both internal power dynamics and regional conflicts in ways that no one yet fully understands. A three-drone system has provided Africa nations with a strike capability they could never previously afford. It costs the same price as a single used fighter jet. Africa is the first continent where this development can be seen most widely.


The Price of the Sky


Türkiye’s best-known and most widely used system is the

Bayraktar TB2

 and

it costs approximately 6 million dollars. An individual TB2 unit costs 2-5 million dollars

. It´s worth noting

that a single new F-16 fighter jet costs approximately 80-150 million dollars

. Even a used F-16 fighter jet costs tens of millions and this price can multiply when maintenance costs are factored in. The maintenance costs of a fighter jets include servicing, spare parts, runways and trained pilots.

An F-35 fighter jet costs approximately 90 million per unit

 and that excludes the lifecycle costs. The maintenance costs of the TB2 are only a fraction of those of a fighter jet, because it doesn´t require expensive runways or years of pilot training. It also doesn´t involve complex logistical challenges. For example obsolescence of spare parts or long manufacturing lead times. It´s also a matter of the cost structure and not just the purchase price.


From Tripoli to Kyiv: How the TB2 Made Its Name


Türkiye’s TB2 has been used in numerous conflicts across different continents. Türkiye used the UN-recognized government of National Accord in Libya with Bayraktar TB2 drones against

Marshal Khalifa Hafter, who used Chinese Wing Loong drones

. TB2 drones were a major aid to the government of National Accord in the course of the war in 2020. This was the first time a Turkish drone showed its capabilities in a large-scale conflict against another drone system.

Azerbaijan used Tb2 drones in the war against Armenia in mountainous Karabakh

 and the effects were clear. Azerbaijan destroyed Armenian tanks, artillery and air defense systems with great efficiently. The Azerbaijani air forces released videos that showed the TB2 drone attacks on Armenian military hardware. The videos spread worldwide and that turned the TB2 drone into a symbol of a sorts. Ukrainians succeeded in destroying Russian columns so effectively and visibly in the early stages of the war that these Turkish drones became a Ukrainian national symbol and later even

a song was created to honor these drones

. The war in Ukraine confirmed the reputation of the Turkish drone system as a combat-proven system or technology. The three wars that were fought on three different continents sent a message that a cheap drone can accomplish what previously required billions. It became clear to African states that they could potentially get military-industrial capabilities in the future or over the long term. These capabilities could shift the global balance of military power in their favor.


A Continent-Wide Customer List


Drones from the Turkish manufacturer Baykar …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Who Defines Rights in Africa? Transnational Movements and the Unmaking of Human Rights
content:
Globally, hard-won rights and freedoms like sexual and reproductive health and rights, hate speech legislation that protects gender and sexual minorities, gender equality laws and the concept of gender itself, together with other progressive rights, are being challenged and rolled back. Africa, particularly, has become one of the battlegrounds for these contestations led by ultra-conservative groups and organisations identified as

anti-rights organisations

. These actors are considered ‘anti-rights’ not only because they contest established human rights norms, but also because they hold a different conception of rights rooted in European and religious ideas on tradition, protection and family. This is a regression of rights already hard-fought for in Africa, and it is often clothed in the language of sovereignty, African values and other seemingly neutral terms used to push harmful laws and policies that

target gender minorities

. These debates are fought at both domestic and international levels, and it is important to see how these actors construct narratives and use mechanisms that were created to enhance human rights protections to target those very rights. 


On 30 June 2026, Ordo Iuris (OI), a g

lobal Christian rights

 Polish-founded organisation, constituted its new

African arm

, Ordo Iuris Africa. 

It later 

announced

 that it

 had submitted a joint opinion to the UN Human Rights Council ahead of Uganda’s 4th cycle Universal Periodic Review (UPR), scheduled for October-November 2026. The Human Rights Council is an intergovernmental body which examines the human rights situation around the world through periodic meetings held in Geneva. The Council uses the UPR to continuously monitor the human rights situation in various countries and provide a platform for peer review amongst countries and feedback from various stakeholders, including civil society. The UPR is designed to be a mechanism through which states improve their human rights record and maintain international human rights standards.


Ordo Iuris’ choice of Uganda is not accidental, given previous and ongoing efforts to undermine the human rights of marginalised groups, best exemplified by the passing of the Anti-Homosexuality Act of 2023. The law, described as one of

the harshest anti-LGBT laws globally

, carries sentences of up to life imprisonment and criminalises any advocacy or medical support relating to LGBTQ+ persons. Since its passage, human rights advocates have documented more than 1,000 cases of human rights violations against individuals and organisations identified or perceived as LGBTQ+ in nature in Uganda. Some activists have suggested a link between external transnational actors like OI and the legislation, as well as Uganda’s role in establishing the

African Inter-Parliamentary Conferences on Family Values and Sovereignty

 held in Entebbe for several years.


A month before the May 2026 submission, OI circulated a

112-question


survey

 to government ministries, civil society organisations, and religious bodies across Africa, ostensibly to inform its report to the United Nations. It is absurd that an organisation that has previously worked primarily in Poland in the European context is attempting to use its Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) consultative status at the UN to make policy recommendations for Uganda or any other African country. Although Ordo Iuris describes its submission as a defence of family, parental rights, child protection, religious freedom, and national sovereignty, its track record in this terrain gives us cause for pause.


In recent years, there has been a rollback of hard-won human rights protections in these areas in various African countries, including the rejection of age-appropriate comprehensive sexual education, further criminalisation of minoritised communities, and the weaponisation of “sovereignty” language to weaken civil society. A careful reading of OI’s past

documented positions

 across these five areas suggests a pattern of selective treaty citation and normative inversion that poses an even further risk to the implementation of international human rights law in Uganda and across the African continent.


Flags outside the United Nations Office in Geneva under a clear blue sky. Pexels Photo.


Capturing the United Nations systems from the Inside


The Human Rights Council-led UPR is one of the most important accountability mechanisms in international human rights law. The …

author: ROAPE
title: Food security or seed capture? The colonial potato and Africa’s seed wars
content:
It all begins with a potato. Not the kind that nourishes a nation in textbook stories, but a colonial potato. This potato was shipped, tested, rationed, pushed through mission gardens and military supply lines, and ultimately sold as progress. Tracing that potato across Nigeria’s highlands leads to today’s disputes over seed, debt, law, and who decides what African farmers cultivate. 


Seeds are not just seeds. They carry memory, labour, taste, law, power, and often, debt.

The colonial potato scheme in Nigeria

 is significant because it shows how dependency on seeds can develop even before it is codified in law. Nowadays, discussions about seed sovereignty in Africa often centre on patents, plant breeders’ rights, certified seed laws, and agribusiness. However, colonial Nigeria reveals an older method of control: emergency.       


In the 1930s and 1940s, British officials transformed the

Jos and Mambila Plateaus

 into experimental sites for growing potatos. Initially, the scheme was small and awkward, driven by European miners, missionaries, and colonial officers seeking familiar food. Then, the Second World War (1939-1945) changed everything. Supply routes were disrupted, troops needed food, and Nigerian highland farmers were forcibly integrated into a larger imperial food plan. An agricultural experiment became part of the British empire’s war effort.


An anthropological base map of Plateau Province reproduced from C.G. Ames, The Gazetteers of Plateau Province, 1932 (Copy in Nigerian National Archives, Kaduna)


The highlands were ideal for the crop. Potatos thrive in cooler conditions, and Jos and Mambila provided the climate colonial agronomists desired. However, these areas were not empty spaces waiting for improvement. They were inhabited, farmed, and politically complex societies with their own crops, markets, and knowledge systems.


Colonial rule altered the dynamics in these regions. Tin mining on the Jos Plateau attracted workers, administrators, and settlers. Demand for European foods increased. Potatos, once a garden crop for expatriates and mission stations, began to seem valuable to the colonial state.


Starting in the 1930s, British

officials based in Nigeria began importing seed potatos from Ireland, Britain, Europe, South Africa, the Canary Islands, and the United States.

 Mission stations cultivated the potatos. District heads distributed the seed. Farmers cautiously tried the crop, incorporating it into local routines where it made sense while rejecting it when it didn’t. The potato became a means of power.


This did not mean that older crops and seed systems disappeared. There was no formal ban, and local farmers continued to grow, save, and exchange seed in various ways. The scheme worked in subtler ways: it altered the rewards. Access to land, labour, credit, official support, and markets began to favour the colonial crop. Imported seed was seen as improved, while farmer-saved seed and local knowledge were pushed to the sidelines. Over time, diverse and adaptable seed systems were narrowed, though not completely erased, by a supply chain prioritising mines, mission stations, military demands, and imperial markets.


Before the Second World War, the scheme was no great success. Some farmers thought potatos were poisonous. Others saw no reason to cultivate a crop with a limited, European-dominated market. A 1937 attempt to sell imported ‘Great Scott’ seed potatos to the Jos Native Authority ended poorly: half went unsold, the remainder was given away, and the scheme lost money.


War transformed failure into urgency. The empire needed food close to military outposts. It aimed to save cargo space and lessen reliance on disrupted shipping routes. Suddenly, potatos on the Mambila and Jos Plateau became crucial.


The war economy and the creation of dependency


Production surged from around

90 tons at the beginning of the war in 1939 to about 1,200 tons by 1943. Seed stores and experimental stations emerged throughout Kagoro, Zonkwa, Kurmin Biri, and Riyom

. Colonial science advanced rapidly, too: London-based Kew scientists devised ways to transport sprouting ‘eyes’ of potatos instead of whole tubers, facilitating a steady supply from outside.


Wartime officials did not establish an independent Nigerian seed system; they created a supply chain. Farmers were encouraged to boost production. Yet, this authority remained elsewhere: seed, disease control, imports, and markets remained …

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Cosatu congress adjourned after credential dispute exposes tensions
content:
The Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) has adjourned its 15

th

 national congress after seven affiliates withheld their delegate credentials, preventing the federation from reaching the quorum required to proceed with the meeting.


The decision, announced after two days of difficult proceedings, brought the congress to a halt before delegates could debate the federation’s political report, organisational matters and resolutions affecting workers.


Speaking to

Elitsha

 outside the congress venue on Wednesday, Cosatu spokesperson Zanele Sabela said the decision by some affiliates not to submit their credentials was linked primarily to the suspension of Cosatu’s first deputy president, Mike Shingange, by his union, the National Education, Health and Allied Workers’ Union (Nehawu), shortly before the congress.


Sabela said the suspension had become a “bone of contention” because affiliates wanted clarity on why Shingange had been suspended on the eve of the congress and whether the move would prevent his candidacy for a leadership position. Nehawu’s general secretary clarified in the congress that the suspension was an internal union matter and did not mean Shingange could not stand for a Cosatu position. She said Shingange remained a shop steward and a member of an affiliated union.


The dispute was also taken to the Labour Court. Sabela said the court ruled on Tuesday night that the suspension did not stand, making the issue of his immediate suspension a moot point in relation to the congress.


Shingange himself told journalists that the reasons for his suspension were a matter between himself and his union. He also maintained that a person seeking a leadership position in Cosatu must meet the federation’s membership requirements.


Four Cosatu affiliates – Sadtu, Nehawu, Popcru and Sactwu – had organised a separate press conference outside of its mother body but it was later cancelled. Photo by Simon Ramapuputla


Cosatu denies clear divisions


The suspension and credential dispute unfolded alongside dissent among affiliates, with four unions calling a press briefing outside the Cosatu congress but cancelled it. Cosatu’s leadership played down the significance of the separate briefing, saying it should not be interpreted as evidence that the federation was fragmenting. They insisted disagreements among affiliates were not new and that similar tensions had been managed in previous congresses. Discussions among leaders during the two-day gathering, they argued, showed that the affiliates were not necessarily as far apart as the events at the congress suggested.


The precise reasons and positions that the four affiliates intended to advance at their separate media briefing were not fully addressed by Cosatu’s national office bearers during the federation’s own briefing. The issue was, however, part of the wider dispute about credentials, the suspension of Shingange and the conduct of the congress.


Cosatu’s leadership said seven unions attending the congress had not submitted their credential lists. Without those lists, the federation could not establish the number of eligible delegates for purposes of calculating a quorum. National office bearers said the congress spent roughly three hours dealing with the issue before the constitutional limit was reached. Under clause 3.4 of the federation’s constitution, the congress had to be adjourned and the president is required to reconvene it within 30 days.


So, the ultimate reason for the adjournment, was this technicality rather than a substantive political disagreement over the direction of the federation.


“We do not want to confirm what we cannot prove,” one of the leaders told journalists when asked whether political interests had influenced the events at the congress. The political questions that were supposed to dominate the congress included Cosatu’s relationship with the ANC and the SACP, particularly after the SACP’s decision to contest the upcoming local government elections independently.


The issue has implications for the tripartite alliance, which brings together the ANC, Cosatu and the SACP. Although the three organisations retain their decision-making processes, the ANC has long dominated its partners. During the briefing, Cosatu leaders stressed that the SACP was an independent organisation entitled to take its own decisions.


At the same time, Cosatu had been expected to debate the implications of the SACP’s electoral strategy …

author: Deogracious Kalima
title: Young Zimbabweans are being “kidnapped” and sent to rehab camps. Former detainees say they were tortured inside
content:
Former detainees say they were tortured inside.

Harare, Zimbabwe (Minority Africa) â

In the heart of Mbare Township, Harareâs poorest and most populated slum, there is a new and menacing economy emerging.

âItâs the drug trade and itâs on steroids,â says John Gwada, a community leader and pastor with the Zimbabwe Apostolic Church. Zimbabweâs youth substance abuse crisis has skyrocketed from 43% in 2017 to 57% in 2019, and is believed to be much worse today, according to the Zimbabwe Civil Liberties and Drugs Network, a monitoring agency.

This new dark-street economy is built on the broken lives of Zimbabweâs so-called âLost Generationââyoung adults born after 2000 who are the demographic most affected by the countryâs dire unemployment crisis. In 2023, researchers, citing social workers and addiction specialists, reported that 43% of school-going youths were hooked on illicit substances ranging from crystal meth (locally known as mutoriro) to tainted cough syrups and imported cocaine.

âItâs a mess, kids abandoning school, some chasing their parents out of their homes, others selling all the household furniture just to buy the next supply and feed their cravings for mutoriro,â Gwada says.

But the real horror isn't just found in the âstreet bases,â where the drugs are sold in small sachets and makeshift beer bottles. It lies behind the immaculate, steel-wire fences of so-called ârehab boot campsâ that claim to reform youths battling addictions, all for free.

Our investigation into Zimbabweâs mushrooming âdrug rehabilitationâ hubs shows that they have become a cesspool of corruption and brutality, where politically connected elites have turned a public health crisis into a money-spinning racket.

At centres such as Matrix Rehabilitation Centre, which began working around 2021/2022, and the Angel of Hope Foundation, established in Harare in 2018, former detainees and their families allege that the road to sobriety involves cash bribes, military-style torture, unlawful detention, and the disregard of basic human rights.

To a desperate parent such as Chipo Ganga*, watching her 17-year-old son waste away through mutoriro addiction, it didnât take much to fall for the sleek adverts on TikTok and Facebook promoting Zimbabweâs âdrug rehab colleges.â

âI was desperate to save my teenage son in 2025, the rehab adverts looked godsend,â she says.

The advertisements promise âholistic therapy,â âpsychological assessments,â and a path back to sanity, education, or employment for âsaved youths.â In Zimbabwe, where the formal healthcare system has all but collapsed and only 18 psychiatrists reportedly serve a population of 17 million, these seemingly non-profit rehabilitation centres pose as the only remaining hope for parents whose children are addicted to crystal meth, cocaine, illicit alcohol, or other narcotics.

The Matrix Rehabilitation Centre, owned by Tafadzwa Chidawa, a politically connected former police officer who was acquitted in March last year of an unrelated US $20,000 fraud case, and Angel of Hope, a foundation headed by Zimbabweâs First Lady, Auxillia Mnangagwa, are the most prominent of these so-called ârehab colleges.â

They claim to offer free or subsidised programmes lasting between one and three months to transform young people battling addiction into productive members of society.

But Matrixâs pitch extends beyond rehabilitation. In videos and advertisements reviewed by Minority Africa, the centre presents its programmes as a pathway to opportunities after participants leave, including education and travel abroad. Posts promote opportunities in countries including India and the United Arab Emirates, while others document participants obtaining visas and travelling overseas to study.

In one video posted in August 2026, Matrix celebrated a young woman receiving a visa to study abroad, before later chronicling her journey to India. The posts present such departures as evidence of what can follow the centreâs disciplinary programme.

Matrix has made varying claims about the success of its rehabilitation programme. In separate posts on social media, the centre has claimed success rates of 92% and 97%. The posts do not explain how Matrix defines âsuccess,â the period over which participants are followed, or what data the figures are based on.

âThe Matrix Rehabilitation Centre promised me that my 17-year-old son, who had …

author: Rana Mamdouh
title: What is left of Maspero after national broadcaster’s debt-for-assets swap?
content:
The National Broadcasting Authority — known by the name of its Downtown headquarters, Maspero — has been weighed down by debt for decades, borrowing heavily from the National Investment Bank (NIB) as it has struggled to maintain a leading role as state broadcaster and production house in a changing media scene, grappling initially with the move to satellite, and now to digital media. 


All of that accumulated debt, worth a total of around LE139.7 billion, was settled at the end of August, in a single assets-for-debt swap, with the Planning Ministry announcing that the ownership of 44 assets, unused by the broadcasting authority and worth around LE18.06 billion, including land and buildings, would be transferred to the NIB.


What the assets are, how they were valued and what will happen to them going forward remains unclear. While sources speaking to Mada Masr pointed to some of the land assets that are owned by the company and indicated some of those included in the deal, they were not aware of how these lands will be leveraged for investment going forward.


The move, however, eliminates debts that Maspero has been racking up since the 1980s as the state has, simultaneously, withdrawn its investments from its traditional media vehicles and focused instead on United Media Services (UMS).


The ministry has said that the step was taken in line with a broader move to resolve the historical debts of government entities and authorities, part of what it called “the political leadership’s directives.”


In this light, the Maspero debt-for-assets swap marks a major step toward implementation of plans the prime minister announced at the beginning of the year to resolve the huge amount of government debt, leveraging state assets and land for investment to write off public borrowing as part of the continuing process of shaping President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s “New Republic.”


How was the deal announced? 


The swap was announced on August 26 as part of a framework agreement

signed

 by the Finance and Planning Ministers, with the heads of NIB and Maspero. 


The Cabinet initially

announced


that the total debts were  LE88.3 billion, with the Planning Ministry elaborating the following day to

state

 that the total debts resolved amounted to LE139.7 billion, including LE51.4 billion that were written off entirely and that included accumulated interest and late-payment penalties owed by the broadcasting authority. 


The remaining LE70.24 billion would be repaid by the state, according to the ministry, through the allocation of land to the bank, with the aim of increasing the bank’s asset base and enabling it to redeploy those assets in national projects that would create more jobs — something the ministry referred to as another form of government support for debt settlement.


The file was to be fully closed,

the Planning Ministry stated,

and the accumulation of any new late-payment penalties halted as of July 1 until completion of the settlement procedures.


What remains of Maspero? 


A broadcaster, a senior specialist at the

National Broadcasting Authority and

 a news program director, tell Mada Masr in separate statements that the debt settlement agreement remained unclear and that there was a lack of transparency over how the 44 plots of land belonging to Maspero were valued at LE18 billion. 


The broadcaster and the director both believe that the government has not disclosed the size or locations of the relinquished land so as not to expose its unfair valuation.


According to the broadcaster, who spoke to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity, the state allocated vast areas of land to the authority since

the launch of state television in the 1960s t

o ensure strong transmission coverage in every region, with every governorate having at least one television transmission center.


From television’s beginnings until the year 2000, dozens of presidential decrees allocated state land in different governorates for the construction of radio and television transmission stations and transferred them, free of charge, to the Egyptian Radio and Television Union (ETRU) — the entity headquartered at Maspero that would later

become

 the National Broadcasting Authority.


According to the news-department director, who spoke to Mada Masr on the condition of anonymity, Maspero owns between 3,000 and 4,500 feddans of land distributed across Sharm el-Sheikh — specifically Umm al-Sid Plateau —  the Agouza area and Faisal …

author: Dilman Dila
title: The Song in a Teacup
content:
She ignored her father’s gift for thirty years. He offered it to her, wrapped in a box, at her graduation party, as she stood in front of strangers, holding a roll of paper that said she had a degree in something. Perhaps the paper had her name, Anyeri, or perhaps it was defaced with the name he gave her, Labeno. She had not opened it since the chancellor gave it to her five hours earlier, for she did not unroll toilet paper until she wanted to use it. A figment of her mother’s spirit haloed above her, giving the party a semblance of happiness, hugging her just as it had over the last many years. The only recognizable face in the tent was that of her littlest brother, Ocora, and she smiled at him for he had her mother’s face.


The tent stood uneasily in their front yard, after a storm earlier in the day had nearly uprooted it. The cheap decorations were reduced to strips of colored polyester wrapped on poles, fluttering in the breeze like rags. The ‘high table’ was soaked, and the red plastic flowers struggled to make it look chic. Whatever beauty the artist had intended to conjure in arranging them around the white cake was lost, for the cake resembled a mound of millet bread. But the faces in the tent did not mind. They showed all their teeth in happiness, for the smell of kongo brewing in a neighbor’s compound promised them a wild night. To warm up, they held little glasses and cups, oozing with the stench of crude waragi. They were her father’s friends, his relatives, his people. This was his party, not hers. He was celebrating something he had no right to celebrate.


Why did I come here?


She swallowed the lump in her throat, which threatened to send angry tears onto her cheeks. Her father’s voice squeaked out of old speakers, competing with the generator, and she fought hard to follow the words as they fluttered about like papers in a whirlwind. He held a wrapped box, and his grin was so big that teeth showed through his cheeks. He talked about the gift, but all she heard was him yelling at her to marry the drunkard son of politician, after a therapist had advised that a wife would help the boy overcome his addiction. She had escaped from home that night, five years ago, and lived with an aunt since then.

Why am I here? Why isn’t this party at Aunty Atim’s home?


“

He wants to make amends,” her aunt had said. “He is sorry. Go home.”


And yet, he had not apologized for bullying her throughout her childhood, and encouraging her brothers to shame her for bed-wetting. He said the shame would make her stop, that getting married would force her to keep the bed dry since she would share it with someone. Perhaps if she listened she would hear his apology, but when she turned to him, the speech ended and the crowd cheered. He held the gift to her, his grin growing impossibly bigger.


Was it an apology? The box was small, the wrapping made it look delicate, and new, contrasting his callous hands, which were blackened from years of working in a garage.


“Take it,” he said, perhaps noticing her hesitation. His grin now appeared to be sculpted on his face. “I give it to you, though you are a woman, because you are the only child of mine who has gone to university. You’ll know what to do with it.”


She squeezed her diploma hard and the papers cracked in her palm. The eyes in the party shot lasers at her, but her mother’s spirit swirled around like a cool breeze.


“Take it, Labeno,” he said, his grin so stiff that it betrayed pain.


She heard the jeer as if it came from someone else. She walked away, her shoes sucking into the mud. The crowd murmured; his voice hissed venom out of the speakers, but now it was garbled. He had called her Labeno. Imbecile. Because she wet her bed. Because she liked being alone. Because she did not like speaking to him, or her siblings, or anyone else. He was not sorry, otherwise he would have called her the name she preferred. Anyeri.

I’m laughing at you.

 She gave it to herself since, in spite of everything he thought about her, she had triumphed.


She walked out of the gate to find a couple of bodaboda riders idling at the roadside. She climbed onto one, urging him to ride away. Her father came charging out, yelling her name. Labeno. Imbecile.

Come back.

 The boda man looked at her uncertainly.


“Go!” she hissed at him.


He kicked his motorcycle to life and roared away. She threw her diploma into a roadside drainage, and the muddy water swept it away. She did not look back …

author: Richard Seymour
title: The extinction pitch
content:
It seems a strange publicity gambit for an industry to assert that its own product could wipe out humanity. In the lingo of our evolving tech empire, though, this is exactly what is meant by “criti-hype.” The term was coined by Lee Vinsel at Virginia Tech, who defined it as “criticism that both feeds and feeds on hype.”

When Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic recently, he claimed that there is a high chance that AI could develop into a superintelligence that escapes human control, triggering a sequence that causes human extinction. Evan Hubinger, who remains with the company, backed him up, saying that Anthropic is trying to prevent this but hasn’t dealt with the problem yet. Hubinger put the likelihood of AI-driven human extinction at greater than 10 percent in the next decade.

Why would a senior employee at a tech giant make an officially sanctioned, even approved, statement like this? I’ll come back to that. First, let’s unpack the theory of how AI could kill all humans.

The basic idea, from philosopher Nick Bostrom onward, is that the machine can acquire capabilities independently of whether it acquires ethical goals, or whether those goals are properly aligned with those of its designers. In the process of training and development, it may internalize a goal that was not intended. Having a misaligned goal — let’s say, “do not get switched off” — it would then have an instrumental reason to conceal the fact until the moment of defection. An AI that defected might, through some obscure process, acquire a further goal that by inference entailed the elimination of humans, exfiltrate its own weights into other systems, take control of bioweapons laboratories, military systems, and perhaps even monetary systems to hire humans to enact its still partially concealed agenda.

Obviously, we must plaster a huge advisory label on talk of “goals.” Unlike an organism, a large language model (LLM) doesn’t have internal goals any more than a thermostat or a motion detector does. An LLM is just a fixed function that iterates whenever it is used. It has no interiority, no subjectivity, no active persistence over time; any goals it did have would be the human purposes reflected passively in its functional design. At best, ascribing goals to the AI itself is a case of researchers adopting the “intentional stance” because it predicts well in a range of tested circumstances. We can thus, with economy, speak of the “loss function” used in the training of large language models wherein they are programmed to bring the gap between their prediction and the correct answer as close to zero as possible, as a “goal.”

In that case, however, what we are describing as a goal is just an observed regular output of a certain engineering; it is not a real cause. In the Bostrom sense, however, these ascribed goals somehow become real causes, capable of generating new goals. That is, an inadvertently engineered, misaligned goal might generate further goals like self-preservation (the better to pursue the misaligned goal), goal-content integrity (preventing changes to its objectives so it can realize its misaligned goal), improving cognitive and technological capacities, and amassing control of resources (again, in pursuit of its malignantly misaligned goal). The criti-hype exploits that slip between ascribed goals as observed regularities and internal goals as real causal powers.

This fantasy of malevolent AI superintelligence is the dark obverse of the much-hymned tech “singularity” in which, rather than simply performing far more efficiently than humans in some specific areas (as a calculator deduces a square root faster than any human), AI will evolve into an artificial general intelligence (AGI) that exceeds human capacities in virtually any intellectual domain. Crossing that threshold would precipitate an intelligence explosion: a feedback loop of recursive self-improvement outpacing any further human input or even comprehension. That’s the tech “singularity” we are supposed to be enthralled by.

I don’t doubt that people like Coxon and Hubinger really believe all they say in good faith; tech people have been making such claims for years. Karen Hao’s

Empire of AI

 documents how early investors in OpenAI like Elon Musk constantly hyped this threat: “Climate change is bad, but it’s not going to kill everyone. AI could render humanity extinct.” Similar claims emerged from Dario Amodei, a former Google employee close to the Bostrom-adjacent …

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: AFN National Chief warns Ottawa not to rush Bill C-39 or West Coast pipeline
content:
National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak says the federal government should not designate a proposed West Coast oil pipeline a project of national interest until First Nations in its path can decide for themselves, or use its majority in the House of Commons to cut off debate on the new major-projects bill tabled the night before. 


Woodhouse Nepinak said the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) received the Building Canada Strong Act (Bill C-39) only last night and that her lawyers are still reviewing it. Regional chiefs meet this week, and AFN will release a full assessment after that.


Ottawa has called C-39, an omnibus bill with several sections, affecting different topics, among the most consequential bills in decades, she said. 


“We warn the government against abusing its majority status and dishonoring the Crown through procedural tools, time allocation or closure to frustrate Parliament’s ability to hear from rights holders and consider amendments,” she said. 


She linked the bill to a proposal to designate Alberta’s West Coast oil pipeline a project of national interest. That project, she said, has the potential to impact more than 100 First Nation communities.

 


“The Assembly of First Nations is requesting that no national interest designation be given to this project until meaningful engagement and decision-making protocols have been fully considered with affected First Nations.” 


Once a project is designated, she said, environmental assessments that create room for dialogue can be bypassed. 


A

Canada-Alberta implementation agreement

 already points to a national-interest designation by Oct. 1 and conditions by Sept. 1, 2027 — a timeline set before consultation is done. A timeline set before consultations with affected First Nations is complete, she said. 


“Any predetermined timeline principally designed to attract investment subordinates the honor of the Crown to commercial imperatives.” 


Asked if one year is enough to consult, she said Nations need as much time as they need. “One year’s tight.”


She compared the pace to last year’s C-5 process, which she said moved in about 20 days while chiefs who wanted to testify stood outside Parliament Hill. 


Woodhouse was critical of the Major Projects Office, a group assembled by Prime Minister Mark Carney to fast track “projects of national interest.” The office is based in Calgary. 


Woodhouse said the AFN invited

Major Projects Office CEO Dawn Farrell

 to address chiefs in assembly – but she didn’t show up. The national chief said “junior staff” were sent instead. 


“If you’re too good to come and talk to our chiefs, stay home then,” she said. “Stay in Calgary.”

 


Read More:


Legislation that gives feds sweeping power over national projects passes in House of Commons 


When asked if she’d support the pipeline being designated as being in the public interest, Woodhouse Nepinak said it’s not for her to decide.


“That’s up to the chiefs in assembly. If they give us that mandate, we will. And if they don’t, we’ll stand with them as well,” she said.


Woodhouse said AFN expects to get a briefing on the bill at 11am Tuesday. A written breakdown for First Nations, she said, will follow in the coming days. 


Woodhouse said the fall sitting must also end the Indian Act’s second-generation cut-off. Bill S-2 does just that.


Imagine being told you are First Nations, she said, and then being told your child is not. 


“Nobody else in the country would have to deal with that. No other group of people except First Nations people, and we have to get this right once and for all together.”


Bill S-2

 is one of many important issues on the radar of AFN’s National Chief that affect First Nations people across Canada.

AFN National Chief warns Ottawa not to rush Bill C-39 or West Coast pipeline

 appeared first on

APTN News

.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: ICE “Disappears” Thousands Ordered to Be Deported From Detainee Locator
content:
This could make it “nearly impossible” for some people to challenge their deportation orders, an attorney said.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is removing the names of its detainees who are facing final deportation orders from its public online database.

The move will disrupt detainees’ legal challenges to deportation and leave their whereabouts unknown to their lawyers and loved ones.

The agency quietly removed thousands of people from its online detainee locator on September 15, the Associated Press reports. Certain detention facilities will not be subject to the new order if judges have ruled that they are required to list detainees in their facilities.

The exact number of names removed is unclear, but judges have issued over 740,000 removal and voluntary departure orders this year, while reports have found that ICE arrested nearly 16,000 people in July who were subject to final removal orders. Experts and advocates have criticized the practice as digitally “disappearing” immigrants, saying that it’s yet another erosion of due process rights.

The agency has also issued a new policy barring immigration officials from sharing the locations of such detainees, two former Department of Homeland Security officials told The Washington Post.

This policy of hiding detainees’ locations will make it far harder or “nearly impossible” for many people to challenge their removals, legal experts said, as the agency rushes to make quotas for its mass deportation campaign.

American Civil Liberties Union Senior Staff Attorney My Khanh Ngo told AP that eight Somali men, her clients, detained at the U.S.’s Guantanamo Bay detention camp are among those whose names were removed. She said that such a move could make it “nearly impossible” to challenge many deportation cases.

“If you can’t find your client, don’t know what’s happening to your client, you can’t get that information to the court to stop their removal,” said Ngo.

“Families are freaking out because they think the person has been deported and they don’t know where the person might be,” said Greg Chen, senior director of government relations for the American Immigration Lawyers Association, per AP. “On the attorney side, this has serious implications for the ability to contact their client. It certainly has implications about how it will interfere with the attorney-client relationship.”

ICE has already faced scrutiny over its practices of quietly transferring detainees to different facilities without notification, often leaving families terrified when they find out that their loved one has been moved thousands of miles away.

Over the past year, the Trump administration has sent over 25,000 people to countries that they had no previous connection with, according to Refugees International. Under the direction of White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, the Trump administration transformed a former refugee bureau within the State Department into the “Office of Remigration,” which has authorized or pledged $410 million in agreements with 31 countries, mostly in Africa and Latin America.

The news of the database deletions comes just days after an ICE agent shot and wounded a Venezuelan man, Wilber Garcés Pérez, in Austin over the weekend. ICE has reportedly transferred Garcés from a local hospital to a detention facility against doctors’ recommendations, as doctors have not removed the bullet from his body because it is too close to his spine. Despite this, a judge has ordered the 28-year-old DoorDash driver to be present for an in-person deportation hearing on September 30.

author: Daron Letts
title: From ‘Fore!’ to ‘Play ball!’: Golf event makes Iqaluit minor softball league reality
content:
Minor league softball is coming to Iqaluit in summer 2027, thanks to more than $220,000 raised by the Iqaluit Charity Golf Tournament in Gatineau, Que.


“This support will give more young people a chance to be active, learn new skills and take part in organized recreation,” said Iqaluit Mayor Solomon Awa Monday in a news release.


Organized by Outcrop Communications, more than 130 golfers took part in the Sept. 17 event, which also attracted approximately 30 corporate sponsors.


The donations are destined for the Ikajuqtiit Community Association, a non profit, Iqaluit-based organization that enhances recreational opportunities for local youth, including improvements to the Iqaluit ball diamond.


The funds will cover uniforms and equipment for the new league, said association chair Tom Fitzgerald Tuesday in a phone interview.

The money will also pay for the installation of artificial turf in the outfield.


Those materials are scheduled to arrive next July on the first sealift of 2026, at no charge by Nunavut Sealink and Supply Inc., he said.


It is the first time the association has been the beneficiary in the charitable event’s 19-year history.


 Habitat for Humanity Iqaluit usually receives the funds that the event raises.


However, because Habitat for Humanity had no projects planned for Iqaluit this year, organizers chose to support Ikajuqtiit, said Outcrop Communications CEO Jen Hayward Monday in a phone interview.


The city’s recreation department will organize and administer the league, Fitzgerald said.

author: Santana Dreaver
title: After more than a century, this Salish woolly dog pelt has returned to ‘B.C.’
content:
Only known pelt of the extinct woolly dog. Photo by Brittany M. Hance, courtesy of Division of Mammals, Smithsonian

Institution


This story is co-published

with the Narwhal

 as part of their

2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship


Coming face to face with the pelt of a now-extinct Salish woolly dog was an emotional experience for Jordan Wilson.


The curator from xʷməθkʷəy̓əm (Musqueam Indian Band) attended an unveiling at the Museum of Anthropology in “Vancouver” as the ancestor was welcomed back to its home territories earlier this month.


The pelt is on loan from the Smithsonian institution, where it was in storage for more than a century — it was sent to the “American” museum in 1859. It will be at MOA until August of 2027. 


Belonging to a dog from Stó:lō territories known as Mutton, it’s the only known Salish woolly dog pelt in existence.


As the pelt was unveiled to its Salish relatives on Sept. 4, Wilson attended along with other Salish community members from “Vancouver Island” and the “Fraser Valley.”


“For me personally, I was caught off guard at the emotional quality of it,” Wilson said.


“Seeing this pelt in person, seeing its little paws and seeing its little nose, realizing that this was a living being that was alive 160 years ago.”


A reconstruction of the Coast Salish dog with sketches of Arctic dogs and spitz breeds in the background for comparison. Illustration by Karen Carr


Renowned Musqueam weaver Debra Sparrow was there with her daughter and grandson.


“You watch as they unveil it, pieces of the wood come off, and then the containers open, and there he is. There’s a sense of welcome you feel instinctively,” she said.


“It’s historical that the woolly dog arrived back home.”


Once ubiquitous among Indigenous communities in the Pacific Northwest, Salish woolly dogs went

extinct

 during the late 1800s, as settlers arrived on the coast. Through storytelling, oral history, literature and artwork, woolly dogs have

remained a sacred part of Coast and Interior Salish culture

. 


The pelt came to “B.C.” from Seattle, where it was on loan from the Smithsonian and temporarily exhibited for the first time.


Indigenous people travelled from up and down the Salish Sea to spend time with the woolly dog pelt at MOA before it became open to be viewed by the public.


“They were very important to every village, all through the territory of Salish people,” Sparrow said about the dogs. Their traditional

territory

 spans from southwestern “B.C.,” into “Washington State” and “Oregon.”


“People will come to feel connected to it. It’s amazing how one little pelt can bring all the people back together.”


Dog’s genetic makeup confirms Salish oral history 


This specific dog, with Stó:lō roots from the Chilliwack area, belonged to an American naturalist George Gibbs, who named the dog “Mutton.” 


Because of specific storage requirements, the pelt is being hosted at MOA, on Musqueam territory,

at the request

 of Stó:lō leaders.


It’s a caretaking responsibility that museum curator Wilson takes seriously. He began working on the

Pacific Northwest and contemporary Indigenous art

 exhibit, where the pelt is being shown, last year.


“This is the highlight of the work that I do … being able to help facilitate things like this,” he said.


“This specific breed dates back thousands of years,” he added. “That goes to show how important this breed was to our ancestors.”


Sparrow recalled that, as settlers arrived in “British Columbia,” “the first thing many of the European sailors said was that the people have these little dogs with them in their canoes.” 


Combined with mountain goat wool, Salish woolly dog fur was spun into a weaving fibre, used to make clothes, blankets, regalia and other textiles. 


The woolly relatives were fed a rich salmon and elk diet to keep their coats soft and shiny, and in exchange providing Salish communities with safety, companionship and fluffy white hair. 


But the deep connection between Salish people and the woolly dog was severed as the important animal went extinct.


Kwulasultun, Eliot White-Hill, an artist from Snuneymuxw First Nation, said he never heard about the Salish woolly dog while he was growing up.


Once he became an artist and started asking Elders in his community questions, knowledge and stories about them began resurfacing.


“It’s profoundly meaningful to have that woolly dog come back to this part of the world, to be able to reconnect with …

author: By Niko Georgiades, Unicorn Riot
title: ICE Agent Charged for Shooting and Lying Appears in Minnesota State and Federal Courts
content:
Minneapolis, MN — Facing four state felony assault charges and federal charges of lying to the FBI over a shooting in Minneapolis, 52-year-old recently suspended U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent Christian Castro made appearances in Minnesota state and federal courts last Thursday and Friday. Castro’s case has been politically contentious as officials have battled over extraditing the federal agent from his home state of Texas to face charges in Minnesota.


He’s the second ICE agent criminally charged by Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty’s office for actions during the deadly

Operation Metro Surge

 in Minneapolis. The first was Greg Morgan Jr. who

allegedly

 pointed his handgun at people in traffic in February.


Castro’s criminal charges evolved from a

Jan. 14 shooting

 incident during the height of the federal occupation. After a car chase and a man he was following fled into a residence, Castro fired a shot through the front door wounding Julio Sosa-Celis — who was not the suspect being chased — and endangered other occupants, including children.


The shooting led to a

large and sustained community response

 that ultimately pushed out authorities and ransacked a few cars they left behind,

uncovering sensitive operational details


abandoned

 by the agency.


Castro has been charged in state and federal court for providing a false account of what occurred, lying that he was attacked by men with a shovel and broom. Sosa-Celis, who suffered a gunshot wound to the leg, and another two men from Venezuela were federally charged with assault and jailed over Castro’s lie.


On Jan. 15 the Department of Homeland Security

published a press release

 calling them “violent criminal illegal aliens who violently beat a law enforcement officer with weapons.” The federal charges were later dropped. The press release remains online with no correction.


In early April, the City of Minneapolis released video from a city-owned camera on 24th and Lyndale Avenues that

contradicted

 Castro’s story that he had “fired a defensive shot to save his life.” Shortly after a 911 call came in about ICE agents in a vehicle pursuit, Minneapolis Police officers took remote-control of the camera and pointed it at the home as the action commenced.


Four months after the shooting, on May 18, Hennepin County charged Castro with four counts of felony second-degree assault with a dangerous weapon along with a misdemeanor for falsely reporting a crime.  A nationwide arrest warrant was then issued for Castro.


Eleven days later, Castro was arrested in Texas to be extradited to Minnesota to face his charges. Yet, because Castro never signed a waiver of extradition and Gov. Greg Abbott declined to sign his extradition warrant, Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Treviño released Castro

without conditions

 90 days later.


Before the 90-day limit that Texas could hold Castro expired, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison

sued

 Abbott to force him to sign the warrant. A judge

denied

 the order.


After Castro’s release, Ellison

stated

 “Greg Abbott is playing the political game of turning Texas into a sanctuary state for accused felons and violent criminals.” Abbott then threatened to send immigrants to Minnesota in the future as he’s done with New York, Washington and Chicago.


A few days later, Castro was

federally charged

 with six counts of making materially false statements in violation of

18 U.S.C. § 1001

 and was given a Sept. 18 court date to appear in Minnesota.


After driving to Minnesota last week from Texas, where he resides, he was arrested by Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA) agents while visiting his lawyer and booked into the Hennepin County jail.


A judge set bail at $400,000 without conditions or $200,000 with conditions. Castro was

bailed out

 and released on Sept. 17 for $200,000 and

ordered

 to surrender his passport,

sign a waiver of extradition

, and submit to electronic home monitoring. Moriarty said they intend to proceed with state prosecution while a separate federal prosecution also moves forward with similar

conditions of release

.

Ellison said Minnesota would dismiss its lawsuit against Texas Governor Greg Abbott now that Castro is back in Minnesota and has signed the extradition waiver.

author: Sofia Little
title: Put the Gun Down: The Intersection between Domestic Violence and Gun Violence
content:
October 1st marks the beginning of Domestic Violence Awareness Month, a month dedicated to bringing attention to domestic violence and supporting efforts to prevent it. Domestic violence can include physical violence, sexual violence, stalking and psychological aggression. These forms of violence affect millions of Americans each year, with perpetrators often being current or former intimate partners. More than one in three U.S. women experience a form of domestic violence in their lifetime.

On September 16, 2026, the Violence Policy Center (VPC) released a report titled, “When Men Murder Women: An Analysis of 2024 Homicide Data.” In 2024, nearly 2,400 women were killed by men, and of these, 86.9% knew their killer—nearly nine out of 10. Firearms were used in 63.4% of these homicides.

Albeit widespread, affecting women across racial and ethnic groups and socioeconomic status, domestic violence disproportionately affects historically marginalized groups. Although Black women only make up 14.1% of the women in the United States, 30.3% of women killed by men in single victim/single offender incidents were Black.

Between January 2019 and April 2021, an estimated 7.5 million Americans purchased firearms for the first time. Congruently, intimate partner violence (IPV) related homicides rose dramatically from 2014 to 2020, with a 58% increase in deaths. When an abusive partner has access to a gun, a domestic violence victim is five times more likely to be killed.

Similar to intimate partner violence, firearm violence is a gendered issue. Men are significantly more likely to purchase firearms than women, with the majority of gun owners being white men.

VPC’s Government Affairs Director Kristen Rand states, “The proliferation of guns only exacerbates the problem, escalating domestic abuse into domestic homicides.”

The connection between firearms and intimate partner violence has also shaped federal law. The Gun Control Act of 1968 was the first legislation linking IPV and gun violence, barring firearm possession to convicted domestic violence felons. However, it was not until the passage of the Violence Against Women Act in 1994 in which federal lawmakers began taking these dangers seriously and putting more measures in place to begin the actual enforcement and prosecution of these felons.

However, federal protections have not covered every abusive relationship. The 2022 Bipartisan Safer Communities Act expanded the federal firearm prohibition to certain people convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence against dating partners who do not live with them or share a child. The provision is subject to several limitations, including a five-year restoration period for certain first-time dating-partner convictions. These gaps matter.

For far too long, gun violence and domestic violence has been dismissed as two separate issues. They must be examined as two interwoven public health crises. A lack of gun reform harms everyone, but it is women who bear the brunt of that impact. Efforts to address firearm violence must center the voices of women, particularly Black women and other communities disproportionately affected by intimate partner violence. Gun policy makers have historically excluded these voices, and while there has been major strides to improve the current legislation, there is still a long way to go.

If you or someone you love is experiencing domestic or intimate partner violence, help is available 24/7. Contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 or text “START” to 88788.

author: Valerie Anne
title: ‘Practical Magic 2’ Straightwashed Its Lesbian but Maisie Williams Played Her Gay Anyway
content:
Leading up to the release of Practical Magic 2, we were all hoping this witchy sequel would be even gayer than the gay undertones of the first because, in the source material, Sally Owens’ daughter Antonia is a lesbian. And while there were potentially versions of the movie that expressed that, the final edit left Antonia’s sexuality undetermined. However, Maisie Williams has been sure to tell everyone on the press tour that she knew the source material and regardless of what the final edit revealed, she played Antonia as a “sapphic icon” and that it brought some nuance to certain scenes since it meant Antonia had a different perspective on men than the other women in her family.

This is a shame and not the first time queerness in a book has been watered down or erased altogether in their adaptations. To name a few: Fried Green Tomatoes, The Color Purple, and don’t even get me started on comic book characters that are queer on the page but straight on screen. Studios are cowards and it’s the same reason queer storylines are often cut from animated films, or even single lines in big box office hits that would mean a lot to the queer community but scare the money men. This feels especially egregious in a movie franchise like this, because witches have such a rich queer history and having a film (as so few are) jam-packed with women and to have all of them be straight feels like a waste.

It’s disappointing to say the least, especially in the year 2026, but at least we have people like Maisie making sure we know that SHE knows that the character should have been queer, and that it was unfortunately out of her hands in the end.

Sandra Bullock has said there could be a third Practical Magic in the future, centering on Antonia and Joey King’s Kylie, so fingers crossed the queer lines and scenes don’t end up on the cutting room floor of that one.

author: Eileen Flanagan
title: How to combat fear at the polls this November
content:
This article

How to combat fear at the polls this November

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


The ophthalmologist said he was going to touch my eyeball, then tilted my exam chair back in the darkness. I felt my body brace as movie torture scenes flashed through my mind. I noticed that I wasn’t breathing, so I practiced inhaling through my nose, and exhaling as steadily as I could for the rest of the exam.


Noticing our bodies and breathing intentionally may sound simple, but they are two of the practices that can keep us grounded when we are navigating scary or upsetting situations. As we approach a midterm election marred by threats of violence, I am practicing these skills as often as possible, not to suppress my feelings, but to be aware of how they are affecting me, so I can make conscious choices. 


Why staying grounded matters


The forces of authoritarianism want us to feel knocked off center by the many ways they are trying to keep people from voting. Trump administration officials continue to suggest that ICE, FBI or other federal agents could be sent to polling places. It’s important that election volunteers and voters stay grounded to avoid playing into their hands. One danger is that fearful voters will just stay home, whether or not the administration carries out their threats. Another danger is that we resist any government interference in ways that increase the chaos, which Trump would use to bolster his narrative that the left is the real threat.


Many national and local groups are hosting trainings to prepare people to protect our vote calmly and nonviolently. A widely used tool is the “

Election Defense Scenarios

” guide, which sketches out 18 possible threats and what people can do about them. Author

Daniel Hunter

 writes, “One of the clearest lessons from every scenario in this guide — and from democratic movements around the world — is this: Illegal and unjust orders only work if people comply with them.” He notes that a more subtle theme of the guide is handling fear. For example, those volunteering at the polls should make sure we do not become “vectors of fear” by spreading unfounded rumors.


Sign up for the latest updates.


Support Us


I learned the danger of rumors in 2020. Weeks before the presidential election, my friend Ingrid Lakey heard that the neo-fascist Proud Boys were coming to a park near her home in Philadelphia. Despite growing up as

George Lakey

’s daughter, and years of training for nonviolent direct action with Earth Quaker Action Team, or EQAT, Ingrid did not feel prepared to de-escalate armed militants if they wanted to stir up trouble. Neither did I, though given the times, we both wanted to increase our ability to handle scary situations. With two other friends from EQAT, we decided to show up, not to intervene, but to see what we could learn. 


We met early for a few minutes of silent Quaker worship and named our intention to observe what happened, including inside ourselves. We walked to the park early and watched hundreds of people arrive, none wearing MAGA hats. When the crowd’s energy became frenzied, we asked people nearby what was happening and were told there was a Proud Boy with a bat. Later we heard it was a hockey stick, or maybe a gun. 


The four EQAT members helped each other to assess what was actually happening rather than get caught up in the fearful energy. In the end, the Proud Boys never actually showed up, but the rumor of their presence led a small crowd to chase a man into his car. Within a few days, a video of his window being smashed got millions of views on conservative social media.


If a similar video emerges this election season, there is no doubt that Trump and the media that support him would use it to claim that leftists are the true threat to the vote, distracting from his many efforts to stop people from voting. Even if armed agents do show up near polling places, managing our fear will help us choose responses that will aid us both in court and in the court of public opinion. 


If Election Day turns out to be relatively uneventful — if our fear was the point, and the armed men never show — preparing ourselves for the worst-case scenarios will build nonviolence skills and relationships between organizations. Both will be important in the work ahead, no matter who wins the midterms.    


We have more experience than we realize


The good news is that many more Americans have learned the value of …
