title: "Yanındayım" dedi, Diyanetin hedefi oldu: İmam Yusuf Kılıç'a Deniz Göktaş soruşturması
content:
Deniz Göktaş'ın Ölü Deniz isimli stand-up gösterisinden

Diyanet, stand-up gösterisi nedeniyle tutuklanan komedyen Deniz Göktaş'a dayanışma mesajı ileten imam Yusuf Kılıç'a soruşturma açtı.

BirGün'den İsmail Arı'nın haberine göre Diyanet İşleri Başkanlığı, Deniz Göktaş'ın ailesine destek mesajı gönderen imam Yusuf Kılıç hakkında soruşturma başlattı. "Ölü Deniz" adlı gösterisinin ardından "Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan'a hakaret" ve "halkı kin ve düşmanlığa tahrik" suçlamalarıyla tutuklanan Göktaş'a "Bir imam olarak yanındayım" diyerek dayanışma gösteren Kılıç, soruşturma kapsamında Ankara'ya çağrılarak savunma verdi. Kılıç, daha önce de 2023 yılında Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan'ın İzmir mitingine cemaati götürmeyi kabul etmediği için disiplin cezaları almış ve İzmir dışına sürgün edilmişti.

Öte yandan 28 Ağustos'ta hakkında tahliye kararı verilmesine rağmen cezaevinden çıkamadan farklı bir suçlamayla tekrar tutuklanan Deniz Göktaş, 28 Eylül'de ilk kez hakim karşısına çıkacak.

Deniz Göktaş, 24 Haziran 2026'da YouTube'da yayımladığı "Ölü Deniz" gösterisinin ardından "Cumhurbaşkanına hakaret" ve "Halkı kin ve düşmanlığa tahrik etmek" suçlamalarıyla tutuklanmış; 28 Ağustos'ta hakkında tahliye kararı verilmesine rağmen cezaevinden çıkamadan farklı bir suçlamayla yeniden tutuklanmıştı.

Göktaş'ın emniyetteki ters kelepçeli görüntüsünün basına servis edilmesinin ardından ailesine destek mesajı gönderen imam Yusuf Kılıç ise daha önce de benzer yaptırımlarla karşılaşmıştı.

Kılıç, 2023 yılında Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan'ın İzmir mitingine cami cemaatini götürme teklifini reddettiği için iki ayrı disiplin soruşturması geçirmiş, kınama ve kademe ilerlemesini durdurma cezaları alarak İzmir dışına sürgün edilmişti.

title: 152 países respaldan a Palestina ante veto de Estados Unidos en Naciones Unidas: Abrumadora mayoría rechaza sanciones
content:
La Asamblea General de la ONU aprobó con 152 votos a favor una resolución que permite a Mahmoud Abbas intervenir por video tras el veto de visados de Estados Unidos. El Estado de Palestina rechazó las sanciones estadounidenses y exigió un diálogo directo para la paz. La Embajada de Palestina en Chile difundió la votación.


Países ONU rechazan por abrumadora mayoría  veto de EE.UU.: 152 países respaldan a Palestina y permiten intervención de Abbas en la Asamblea General


La votación en la ONU


La Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas aprobó este jueves 17 de septiembre de 2026, con una abrumadora mayoría de 152 votos a favor, una resolución que permite al presidente palestino, Mahmoud Abbas, intervenir en la Semana de Alto Nivel a través de un mensaje grabado en video, según informó la Embajada del Estado de Palestina en Chile a través de su cuenta de X.


 ABRUMADORA VOTACIÓN EN LA ONU: 152 PAÍSES RESPALDAN A PALESTINA ANTE EL VETO DE ESTADOS UNIDOS


En una contundente demostración de multilateralismo y respaldo internacional, la Asamblea General de la Organización de las Naciones Unidas (ONU) aprobó por una abrumadora mayoría…

pic.twitter.com/RemakWXfCT


— Embajada del Estado de Palestina en Chile (@embpalestinacl)

September 18, 2026


La medida surge como respuesta directa al bloqueo político ejercido por Estados Unidos, que denegó el visado a la delegación palestina para impedir su presencia física en la sede de Nueva York, de acuerdo con la misma fuente.


 LA COMUNIDAD INTERNACIONAL RECHAZA EL VETO DE VISAS DE ESTADOS UNIDOS A PALESTINA


 Mira el momento en que la comunidad internacional votó abrumadoramente en contra de la decisión de Estados Unidos de negar visas a los funcionarios palestinos para participar en la sesión…

pic.twitter.com/RpYBGmQuh8


— Embajada del Estado de Palestina en Chile (@embpalestinacl)

September 18, 2026


En un comunicado oficial emitido el 17 de septiembre de 2026 desde Ramallah, el Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores y Expatriados del Estado de Palestina expresó su rechazo a la decisión de Estados Unidos de prorrogar las restricciones a la concesión de visados de entrada a funcionarios de la Autoridad Nacional Palestina y a miembros de la Organización para la Liberación de Palestina (OLP). El documento califica la medida como “injustificada” y advierte que “contradice los esfuerzos desplegados para restablecer la confianza, desarrollar las relaciones palestino-estadounidenses y propiciar el clima político necesario para la aplicación de la solución de dos Estados”.


Los resultados de la votación


La Embajada de Palestina en Chile detalló los resultados de la votación: 152 países a favor, incluyendo “un amplio consenso global que defiende el derecho de Palestina a hacerse escuchar en los foros internacionales”; 4 abstenciones de Colombia, Honduras, Panamá y Perú; y 3 votos en contra de Estados Unidos, Israel y Paraguay. La resolución permite al presidente Mahmoud Abbas dirigirse a la Asamblea General mediante un mensaje pregrabado, garantizando la participación palestina pese al veto migratorio.


Las palabras del embajador Riyad Mansour


Frente al bloqueo de visados, el embajador palestino ante la ONU, Riyad Mansour, envió un mensaje desde la sede multilateral: “El hecho de que se nos hayan denegado las visas no significa que el pueblo palestino y su liderazgo no estén presentes. Están presentes, en primera línea y en el centro, y lo estarán hasta que pongamos fin a esta ocupación ilegal y permitamos que el consenso global de la comunidad internacional logre una solución de dos Estados”.


Mansour también “agradeció a los países que votaron a favor” y “condenó la denegación del ‘derecho legítimo’ de la delegación a participar”, según recogió la Embajada palestina.


El rechazo a las sanciones


El comunicado del Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores palestino rechaza la afirmación de que el recurso del pueblo palestino a las Naciones Unidas, la Corte Internacional de Justicia y la Corte Penal Internacional constituya un acto que socave la paz. Por el contrario, el documento sostiene que “acudir a las instituciones internacionales y al derecho internacional es un derecho legítimo del Estado de Palestina y un medio pacífico y jurídico para proteger a nuestro pueblo y sus derechos”.


El texto subraya que “no puede equipararse con las políticas de ocupación, colonización, anexión y desplazamiento forzado”.

author: David Swanson
title: Charlottesville Marked the International Day of Peace
content:
By the

Charlottesville Center for Peace and Justice

, September 21, 2026


Charlottesville Center for Peace and Justice held a rally at the Downtown Mall on Monday, marking the International Day of Peace. The rally was moved under the Charlottesville pavillion due to rain.


A focus was CCPJ’s

petition

 urging the City Council of Charlottesville to pass a resolution opposing current wars.


Devon Sproule led the rally in song.


Speakers included Lena Seville, Virginia Rovnyak, Alexandra Kedrock, David Swanson, and Jeff Fogel.


Following the rally, participants attended a City Council meeting. Among those who spoke to the City Council in support of a resolution were David Swanson, Lena Seville, and

Joanie Freeman.


Videos here

.


David Swanson’s remarks at the rally were as follows: 


We recently learned that some months ago the U.S. military came within moments of so-called intercepting a Chinese ship. The U.S. military had used so-called artificial intelligence to determine that the ship was carrying some sort of nuclear technology, but at the last minute found the modicum of natural intelligence to realize its robot had got it wrong.


If AI is a threat to life on Earth, it needs to take a number and get in line behind existing threats bizarrely erased by claims that an omnicidal threat is something new under the sun, threats like climate collapse, disease epidemics, and nuclear war. If AI kills us all, it will likely be in combination with one of the pre-existing threats. And long before AI can have a chance to kill us all through superior malevolence, we will first have to survive the danger of humans teaming up with AI to kill us all through magnified stupidity.


The greatest threat right now is the president of the United States who continues to publicly threaten genocide in Iran, to erase a civilization, to blow up a whole nation. This might be the single worst crime in the history of the world, possibly killing 90 million people plus many millions or billions more depending on the types of weapons used and the resulting escalation — quite likely including nuclear war on a scale to impose nuclear winter on the globe. Yet there are larger protests to protect the Kennedy Center. Yes, I, too, love the Kennedy Center. But another sign that our priorities are askew is that when Trump talks of making a deal with Iran, various Democrats in Congress accuse him of “chickening out” and of making a terrible deal. Well, of course it would be a terrible deal — at least for Trump and his oil-company funders, but not more terrible than war.


Does anybody here remember when they used to pretend that wars had nothing to do with oil? And they weren’t about profits or power or the egos of sadistic dictatorial buffoons? Remember? They were very, very serious. People were being bombed into democracy. Towns were being reluctantly leveled as proper and proportionate strategic steps to meet the benchmarks of solemn statesmen. I’m glad all of that’s gone. I’m glad our national court jester makes his motivations as clear as a preschooler. It’s one reason we now have a huge majority against the wars. Another is the sheer idiocy of making a war be about reopening a waterway that was closed by the war. Remember when we thought making a war be about finding imaginary weapons was the dumbest possible idea?


And yet, I also remember when a smaller percentage of us opposed wars and we nonetheless packed the streets and pressed for change. We gave the war on Iraq such a bad name that they told us we were ill. We had the Iraq Syndrome, which was their name for a reluctance to support more wars. While that illness lasted we prevented a big war on Syria and even a war on Iran for a while, and even the election of people who’d voted for the war on Iraq. Now we have a larger majority than ever against the wars. The Iran war became unpopular faster than any past war. But the warmongers are grinning ear to ear and asking

What, Me Worry?

They’ve got us all fooled with a different lie, the lie of our powerlessness, the lie that we can do nothing whatsoever, or we can vote, we can go home and cry, or we can go shopping, or we can vote really really hard. author: CMI Argentina
title: Sobre el acuerdo firmado por Facundo Jones Huala con la justicia en la causa en su contra
content:
Desde la Gremial de Abogadxs, a cargo de la defensa del Lonko, explicaron los motivos y alcances del acuerdo firmado en el marco de un juicio abreviado, que fue homologado por el juez federal de Bariloche, a partir del que Jones Huala cumplirá una condena de 5 años y dos meses.


Compartimos comunicado de la Gremial:


LA GREMIAL INFORMA QUE EN LA CAUSA CONTRA EL LONKO FACUNDO JONES HUALA SE HA FIRMADO UN ACUERDO DE CONDENA DE 5 AÑOS Y 2 MESES EN JUICIO ABREVIADO. EL ACUERDO FUE HOMOLOGADO POR EL JUEZ FEDERAL DE BARILOCHE.


SIN ARREPENTIMIENTOS NI PEDIDOS DE DISCULPAS.


A partir de una propuesta realizada por la fiscalía de Bariloche hace varias semanas, se llevó adelante una serie de conversaciones entre las dos partes que, desde el principio y hasta el final, incluyeron siempre a Facundo.


Hasta último momento la fiscalía insistió en que Facundo se responsabilizara en los términos del art. 210 bis del Código Penal (que penaliza la Asociación Ilícita para poner en peligro la Constitución Nacional).


A cambio ofrecía una pena de 5 años y medio.


Tanto Facundo como los defensores nos negamos a aceptar esa imputación. Además de no corresponder en lo más mínimo, significaba claramente abrir la puerta a graves e incluso imprevisibles consecuencias. (judiciales y políticas).


Una de ellas hubiera sido el permanente intento de la Fiscalía de probar “ramificaciones internacionales” entre la CAM de Chile y la RAM de Argentina.


Además, en caso de ir a juicio oral por esa acusación, el 210 bis supone una pena entre 5 y 20 años de prisión.


Finalmente, la fiscalía aceptó encuadrar la acusación en los términos del art. 213 bis Cod. Penal (penaliza a los miembros de una organización transitoria que tenga por objeto imponer sus ideas por la fuerza, por el solo hecho de ser miembros).


Esta acusación estuvo desde el primer momento y, junto con la apología del delito, fue el origen de la causa a partir de la presentación de su libro.


La fiscalía, por su parte, dejó sin efecto todas las apelaciones y recursos para que Facundo sea devuelto al Penal de Rawson.


En los hechos, y más allá de los términos y las expresiones propias de la ley penal, esto significó hacerse cargo de lo que Facundo se ha hecho cargo desde siempre: que la RAM existió y que él fue miembro de la misma.


Eso, y nada más que eso, es lo que asumió Facundo en este acuerdo con la Fiscalía.


La ley penal y Facundo no califican de la misma manera a la organización, aunque ambos partan de las expresiones con que Facundo y la propia RAM expusieron sus propósitos, su razón de ser y sus objetivos.


Obviamente, son dos puntos de vista diametralmente opuestos.


Pero cuando uno está sometido por el estado a un proceso penal, es el estado el que elige los términos.


Nosotros tenemos en claro que el juicio abreviado es ni más ni menos que una herramienta de extorsión de la que disponen los fiscales y que es eficaz, justamente, porque nadie puede confiar su inocencia en los jueces argentinos.


No hay ni habrá ninguna garantía que Facundo fuera a tener un juicio objetivo e imparcial, más bien todo lo contrario como se viene demostrando con su causa y con otras.


A la Gremial le duele que Facundo tenga que estar cumpliendo condena por varios años más. Es claramente injusto.


Pero los miembros de la Gremial tenemos, en muchos casos, largos años de experiencia en la lucha política y sus consecuencias penales, tanto como luchadores e integrantes de Organizaciones, tanto como presos en condiciones externas, como así también en el rol de abogados defensores.


La Gremial no se encuentra en condiciones, de ninguna manera de asumir la responsabilidad de presumir que, en casos como el de Facundo, se puede ir a juicio y salir absuelto.


Con Facundo vienen aplicando audiencia tras audiencia lo que llamamos “el Derecho Penal del enemigo” y no garantizamos que no lo sigan haciendo, especialmente en un juicio oral.


Para él, ir a juicio por el art. 210 bis significaba casi seguramente afrontar una condena de más de 10 años.


No estábamos en condiciones de decirle, y no le dijimos, “jugate 10 ó 12 o 15 años de tu vida a que podés ganar el juicio”.


Ya hemos dicho hasta el hartazgo qué es lo que pensamos de las leyes y el sistema judicial del Estado Argentino.


Lo decimos por un conocimiento general de cómo son las cosas en los Tribunales, pero particularmente porque en nuestra experiencia como defensores de miembros del Pueblo Mapuche, todos los condenados lo fueron …

author: CMI Argentina
title: Cambiar un empleo formal por la informalidad cuesta hasta un 27,8% del salario real
content:
Un estudio de C-P Consultora reveló que los trabajadores que abandonan un puesto registrado para pasar al cuentapropismo pierden casi un tercio de su poder adquisitivo, mientras que quienes caen en el empleo no registrado de la informalidad sufren un recorte del 13,9%. La contracara: conseguir un empleo formal es la vía más efectiva para recomponer ingresos, con mejoras de hasta el 34,3%.


El mercado laboral argentino atraviesa un proceso de precarización estructural que se profundizó en los últimos años. Según un informe de C-P Consultora, los trabajadores que cambian un empleo formal por la informalidad pierden hasta un 27,8% de su salario real. El estudio, elaborado a partir del seguimiento de trabajadores de entre 18 y 65 años a través de ocho paneles de la Encuesta Permanente de Hogares (EPH) entre 2023 y 2025, evidencia que abandonar un empleo asalariado formal genera caídas sustanciales en la capacidad de compra. El golpe más severo lo sufren quienes terminan trabajando por cuenta propia, con un retroceso promedio del 27,8% en sus ingresos reales.


El informe detalla que los trabajadores que migran de un puesto registrado a un empleo no registrado sufren un recorte del 13,9% en su poder adquisitivo, mientras que trasladarse desde el sector privado registrado hacia el sector público representa un descenso promedio del 5,4% en la remuneración. En contraste, aquellos asalariados del sector privado que lograron conservar su puesto registrado experimentaron una mejora promedio del 2% en sus ingresos reales. “Lo que está creciendo es una forma de trabajo que es aún más precaria que la del asalariado informal”, advirtió Pablo Moldovan, analista de C-P Consultora, al puntualizar que se trata de ocupaciones vulnerables caracterizadas por la ausencia de un salario fijo, jefe, lugar físico de trabajo y cobertura de obra social.


El contexto agrava el diagnóstico. La desocupación alcanzó el 7,9% en el segundo trimestre de 2026, mientras que el empleo no registrado abarca al 45% de los trabajadores. Según el informe, el aumento del trabajo en negro y del cuentapropismo oculta una recomposición hacia abajo de la estructura ocupacional, impulsada por la necesidad de más integrantes del hogar de salir a buscar ingresos para llegar a fin de mes. Se trata de una dinámica que ya fue advertida por otros estudios: el Centro de Economía Política Argentina (CEPA) había señalado que la creación de empleo en el último año se concentró casi exclusivamente en el sector informal.


La contracara del informe es que acceder a un puesto formal es la vía más efectiva para recomponer los ingresos. Los cuentapropistas que lograron conseguir un empleo privado registrado al cabo de un año aumentaron sus ingresos reales un 34,3%, y la transición desde un empleo asalariado no registrado hacia el sector privado formal implicó una suba del 31,6% en la remuneración real. Esta asimetría entre la pérdida que implica caer en la informalidad y la ganancia que representa acceder a un empleo registrado refuerza la centralidad del trabajo formal como herramienta de movilidad social y de recuperación del poder adquisitivo.


El escenario se enmarca en un mercado laboral que acumula más de un año de caída del empleo formal privado. Según datos de la Secretaría de Trabajo, el empleo asalariado registrado acumuló doce meses consecutivos de retrocesos hasta junio de 2026, y la cantidad de trabajadores formales del sector privado se ubica en niveles similares a los de julio de 2016. En paralelo, el salario mínimo real acumuló una caída del 40,5% entre noviembre de 2023 y julio de 2026, lo que lleva a que su valor actual sea inferior al de 2001, antes del colapso de la convertibilidad, según un informe del Instituto Interdisciplinario de Economía Política (IIEP) de la UBA.

title: Kicillof encabezó su primer acto político de cara a las presidenciales 2027
content:
Fue en la sede de la Universidad Tecnológica Nacional de Avellaneda como cierre del Plenario Federal del Movimiento Derecho al Futuro que lidera el gobernador bonaerense.


Axel Kicillof encabezó su primer acto político de cara a las elecciones presidenciales de 2027. En un discurso de más de una hora, que leyó íntegramente, el gobernador llamó construir una alternativa nacional para cambiar el rumbo económico de la Argentina.


Lo que está viviendo nuestro pueblo, entendemos que no se va a salir de esta situación tan dramática, ni con jugadas mágicas, ni con improvisaciones, lo que se necesita es mucho trabajo, mucha participación, muchos encuentros y estamos hoy dando un paso importantísimo para que eso ocurra.


Además, enfatizó: “Una alternativa nacional, déjenme decirles, no se construye desde una oficina, por eso venimos recorriendo las provincias, por eso nos pone tan contentos, felices ver militantes y dirigentes hoy de nuestra patria”.


Por último, el mandatario bonaerense aseguró que “con Milei, en el país se está produciendo una verdadera catástrofe, la necesidad y el desafío también va quedando claro, el año que viene tenemos que cambiar el rumbo económico de la Argentina”.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Democratic States Cave on Paramount Merger Lawsuit in Win for Billionaire Owners
content:
The settlement will place CNN and CBS News under control of a group chosen by the conglomerate’s board of directors.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

A coalition of Democratic states and Paramount reached a settlement in a lawsuit against its proposed $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery on Monday, paving the way for one of the largest media mergers in history — and a massive consolidation of power over a huge swath of the entertainment and news industries under the conservative billionaire Ellison family.

The antitrust lawsuit was the last major obstacle for the deal, which has already been blessed by the Trump administration. Attorneys general from 12 states had sued to block the merger, which leading California Attorney General Rob Bonta had called “unlawful,” amid a flurry of antitrust concerns from prominent Hollywood figures and press freedom groups. The Writers Guild of America’s (WGA) lawsuit against the merger was also settled on Monday, with the union saying that its members could not afford to continue the legal battle on their own.

The merger will grant widespread power to a company that would effectively control CNN; CBS News; and, in all, roughly 30 percent of wide-release theatrical film distribution and basic cable channel licensing. It amounts to roughly 20 percent of Americans’ television watching time — all conglomerated under the leadership of Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison. David Ellison is a major ally to Trump and son of Oracle CEO Larry Ellison, who has personally donated millions to Israel’s military; Paramount had once dubiously suggested that opposition to the merger was a result of antisemitism.

David Ellison, who thanked California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) in his statement celebrating the deal, has said that the merger is expected to go through in two weeks. Pro-Israel David Zaslav, the president of Warner Brothers Discovery — an entity that’s a conglomerate on its own, formed as a result of several other contentious mergers — is slated to receive $660 million from the merger, which would likely make him a billionaire.

Under the settlement, the newly formed megacorporation will be obligated to comply with several provisions, including the theatrical release of 30 films a year (something Paramount already independently pledged to do last year); a requirement for separate negotiations for cable channel distribution; management of two historic production lots; and an apparent commitment to domestic filmmaking.

The deal also includes a supposed commitment to a “News Editorial Independence Board” for the management of CNN and CBS, which will comprise of former or current journalists who are hand-picked by the conglomerate’s board of directors. News analysts and advocates have already cast doubt on the idea that the board will be effective, however, as past efforts to form similar such structures have failed.

David Ellison has already demonstrated a willingness to steer the news toward the right wing in his appointment of right-wing media figure Bari Weiss as CBS’s editor-in-chief last year. Meanwhile, press freedom advocates on Monday also urged David Ellison to oppose Trump’s recent ban on CNN in the press pool, noting his silence on the issue despite his stated commitments to press freedom.

Some of the world’s most repressive regimes will have a say at the company, too. The settlement comes just days after the Federal Communications Commission approved Paramount Skydance’s plan to allow the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates to have a 49.5 percent equity stake in the newly merged company.

The deal immediately faced a deluge of criticism after it was announced on Monday, with critics saying that it will have “devastating” results for the nation’s media landscape and press freedom at a time of massive repression under the Trump administration.

“Today, billionaires have yet again bribed, censored, and bullied their way to the top,” said Alvaro Bedoya, a senior advisor for the American Economic Liberties Project. “As a result, a billionaire media conglomerate closely allied with the president will soon own one of its closest rivals, including some of the nation’s most critical news outlets.”

author: Amy Goodman
title: US Deportees Sent to Equatorial Guinea Decry Inhumane Conditions, Imprisonment
content:
Individuals deported there under “third-country agreements” have been denied the ability to contact their families.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Two men deported from the United States to Equatorial Guinea were arrested by local police forces and transferred to a prison earlier this month, in apparent retaliation for speaking out about conditions they faced in the Central African country. Samson Birhane, who is from Eritrea, and Ahmed Soliman, a gay asylum seeker from Egypt, were both deported by the Trump administration despite U.S. immigration courts granting them protections.

On September 11, police forces arrived at Hotel Bamy in the city of Malabo, where more than two dozen people have been confined after their deportation from the United States to Equatorial Guinea, a country they have no ties to, as part of President Trump’s secretive “third-country” agreements. Birhane and Soliman say they were arrested and taken to prison for speaking out about the inhumane conditions endured by U.S. deportees at the hotel and threats by armed forces. While confined at the hotel, U.S. deportees have decried denial of medical care and legal assistance, and abuses they’ve described as psychological torture.

“Starting in November 2025, … the United States started this horrendous policy of sending immigrants not from Equatorial Guinea to Equatorial Guinea, a country that the U.S. knows very, very well that is a human rights violator,” says human rights lawyer Tutu Alicante. “The State Department reports that the U.S. has been putting out for the last three decades are consistent about the fact that Equatorial Guinea uses torture, uses incommunicado detentions, and often extrajudicial killings of people that it keeps in prison.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

Amnesty International is calling for the release of two men deported from the U.S. to Equatorial Guinea. They were arrested by local police forces there and transferred to a prison earlier this month. The men are Samson Birhane, who is with — who is from Eritrea, and Ahmed Soliman, a gay asylum seeker from Egypt, who was living in Arizona when he was detained by ICE. Both of them were deported by the Trump administration despite U.S. immigration courts granting them protections.

On September 11th, police forces arrived at Hotel Bami in the city of Malabo in Equatorial Guinea, where more than two dozen men and women have been confined after their deportation from the U.S. This is a country, Equatorial Guinea, they have no ties to, part of a secretive so-called third-country agreement.

It’s believed the two men were arrested and taken to prison for speaking out about the inhumane conditions endured by U.S. deportees at the hotel and threats by armed forces. Just days before their arrest, video footage obtained by Reuters showed guards pointing their guns at a group of U.S. deportees inside the hotel after a Cuban man asked an officer to return his confiscated cellphone so he could contact his family and lawyer. This is Ahmed Soliman describing what happened that day. This was before his arrest. He’s since been taken to a prison in Malabo.

AHMED SOLIMAN: Yesterday morning, another detainee here has had his phone confiscated for about two weeks, and he went downstairs to speak to the officers to try to have them call the director in charge, who is also their boss. Like I said, he hasn’t had his phone for about two weeks. He hasn’t been able to talk to his loved ones, his family, his lawyers, which in turn is a violation of human right laws. We are not criminals in this country. We deserve rights. We have rights, and we know our rights. So, after about 15-20 minutes of him being downstairs pleading with these officers to call the director, these officers were completely disregarding his pleas, his requests, and were just ignoring him, not giving him the time of day, were sitting on their phones, not even listening to him. …

That’s when they then took us inside the hotel, where they pointed their guns at me. They cocked their guns, took it off of safety and pointed their guns at me, telling me to get on my knees with my hands up, where I had to remain in that position for, you know, 10-15 minutes, while there was chaos going on in the hotel. … …

author: Sufia Khalid
title: The National Security Exception Was Never Going to Stop at Prosecuting Muslims
content:
For 25 years, the US ran a parallel legal system targeting Muslims. It now reaches activists, immigrants, and the left.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

For 25 years, the US ran a parallel legal system largely for Muslims. It now reaches immigrants and the left.

Less than two weeks after the September 11, 2001, attacks, President George W. Bush told Congress that the war on terror “begins with al Qaeda, but it does not end there.” Twenty-five years later, his line reads as a confession: the war on terror was designed to have no borders and no end, and the legal machinery built to wage it at home was drafted in the same way.

In my work as a federal criminal defense and constitutional law attorney, I defend people unjustly prosecuted by that machinery. Until recently, most of my clients were Muslim. What their cases demonstrate is that after 9/11, the United States built a separate system of justice — a national security exception to the Constitution — that was largely tested on a population that was demonized by both the state and the media. While non-Muslims were assured it would never apply to them — and were repeatedly told not to worry about the creeping encroachment of the state if they had nothing to hide — that assurance has expired.

The national security exception to the Constitution operates through a variety of mechanisms: statutes vague enough to criminalize charity and speech; informants and undercover agents who manufacture crimes they later “disrupt”; classified evidence defendants cannot see; mass surveillance; and a sentencing enhancement that categorizes even first-time, nonviolent defendants as hardened career offenders. Each element was justified as an emergency measure, but none of them has expired.

In 2004, Justice Sandra Day O’Connor wrote in Hamdi v. Rumsfeld (a Supreme Court case that found that American citizens detained from an active combat zone as enemy combatants retain the right to due process and a meaningful opportunity to challenge the factual basis of their detention before a neutral decision-maker) that “a state of war is not a blank check for the President when it comes to the rights of the Nation’s citizens.” But for Muslims in U.S. courtrooms, it has functioned as one. Sixty years earlier, dissenting in Korematsu v. United States, in which the Supreme Court upheld the internment of over 120,000 Japanese Americans during World War II, Justice Robert Jackson warned that a principle of discrimination, once blessed by the courts, “lies about like a loaded weapon, ready for the hand of any authority that can bring forward a plausible claim of an urgent need,” and that “every repetition imbeds that principle more deeply in our law and thinking and expands it to new purposes.”

We have been living inside that warning, with the guise of “national security” as the ever-prevailing “urgent need.”

The statutes criminalizing the “material support” of terrorism sit at the center of the exception. Under the U.S. federal criminal code, Section 2339B of Title 18 makes it a felony to provide “material support or resources” to any group the secretary of state designates a foreign terrorist organization, with no requirement that the defendant intended to further violence or that anything they provided was ever used for such purpose. Section 2339A criminalizes “material support” of terrorist acts, which includes property damage, for anyone — no organizational affiliation, foreign or domestic, is necessary. After 9/11, Congress added “expert advice or assistance,” to the definition of material support, extended the law to “any property, tangible or intangible, or service,” and increased the maximum sentence for Section 2339B to 20 years. In Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project, the Supreme Court held in 2010 that even teaching members of designated groups to peacefully use international law and petition the United Nations could be prosecuted as support for terrorism.

author: Natalia Viana
title: “Modelo Bukele” no Brasil significaria 4 milhões de brasileiros na cadeia
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a newsletter Xeque na Democracia, enviada toda segunda-feira, 12h. Para receber as próximas edições,

inscreva-se aqui.


Ele estava em um debate na Europa explicando como funciona a política de

segurança pública

 do presidente de El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, quando foi interpelado por um empresário brasileiro, que lhe disse: “precisamos de um Bukele no Brasil”. 


Dada, que conhece o Brasil e fala português, pediu mais explicações. “Qual é o problema que enfrentamos na segurança pública?”

O interlocutor explicou que as favelas aqui, assim como as comunidades pobres em El Salvador, são dominadas por organizações criminosas. O jornalista respondeu: “Então é fácil resolver o problema. Basta lançar bombas nas favelas”. Surpreso, o brasileiro retrucou: “Mas não podemos fazer isso”. “E por quê?”, perguntou Dada. “Porque iríamos matar gente inocente”.


“Pronto, então você já entendeu o que é o modelo Bukele”.


Carlos Dada é meu amigo desde a fundação da

Agência


Pública

, e é uma das pessoas que conhece mais profundamente o que significa na prática o tal “modelo Bukele” defendido por vários candidatos da direita. À frente do

El Faro

, primeiro site jornalístico do continente e um dos mais premiados, ele viu o número de encarceramentos do país se tornar o maior do mundo em apenas alguns anos, relativamente à população. 


Hoje, 1 em cada 50 salvadorenhos estão na prisão, ou 120 mil dentre 6 milhões de cidadãos. Se transportado para o Brasil, isso significaria mais de 4 milhões de brasileiros na cadeia.

 Atualmente temos mais de 960 mil presos, terceira maior população carcerária do mundo. 


O “modelo Bukele” é defendido por empresários como aqueles da cúpula da Fiesp que, em 31 de agosto

, fez um evento com candidatos da direita

, entre eles o ex-juiz Sérgio Moro, candidato ao governo do Paraná pelo PL e o candidato a Senador por SP, Guilherme Derrite (PP) para ouvirem o ministro de Segurança Pública de El Salvador, Gustavo Villatoro. O presidente da Fiesp, Paulo Skaf, disse na ocasião: “O que precisamos como sociedade é dar o apoio que for necessário para que um novo governo possa fazer as transformações que o Brasil necessita e para que as pessoas possam sentir segurança” – reforçando sua torcida por um “novo governo”.


O que o empresariado de São Paulo não sabe é que o “sucesso” da redução imediata da criminalidade pelo governo Bukele não se deveu a um plano milagroso,

mas a um acordo com os líderes das organizações criminosas mais conhecidas, como a Mara Salvatrucha. Quem descobriu detalhes destes acordos foi Carlos Dada e sua equipe.


“O acordo incluiu a libertação ilegal e em segredo de alguns chefões que já estavam presos. Implicou também o alívio de medidas em cadeias de segurança máxima. Seus parentes sim podiam visitá-los, eles tinham mais horas livres, tinham muitas saídas a hospitais onde se reuniam com seu pessoal”, explica.

Do lado dos criminosos, a promessa era baixar o número de homicídios e garantir o voto a Bukele em suas comunidades.

 


A equipe do El Faro recebeu vazamentos de documentos mostrando como as “saidinhas” de chefões se tornaram muito mais frequentes, assim como as visitas. E eles obtiveram áudios nos quais um ministro de Bukele pessoalmente confessa ter tirado o chefão chamado Crook da cadeia e o levado em seu carro até a Guatemala. A viagem foi confirmada por um registro insuspeito: durante todo o trajeto a namorada do criminoso tirou fotos e postou no seu Instagram, tentando esconder o namorado. “Mas apareciam os braços e as tatuagens dele”, explica Dada. 


A coisa ficou ainda mais escancarada, explica Dada, quando alguns destes líderes foram presos no México e extraditados para os Estados Unidos. Dada e seus colegas conseguiram comprovar que a própria justiça americana beneficiou estes criminosos – a pedido do governo Trump. 


“Os criminosos estavam para ser julgados nos EUA, e alguns assinaram acordos como testemunhas protegidas e revelaram este pacto com Bukele. Dá um

Fast Forward.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Bessent Says New US Sanctions Will “Shut Down” All Iranian Airlines Worldwide
content:
The announcement comes after Trump made his latest genocidal threat to “blow the entire nation up.”

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that the U.S. is slated to unleash new sanctions aimed at cutting off Iranian airlines from global travel, once again leveraging the U.S.’s vast power over the global financial system to further isolate Iran as the energy crisis spurred by the war rapidly worsens.

“On September 23rd, all the Iranian airlines, all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world,” said Bessent in an interview with CNBC on Monday.

He said that the sanctions would be imposed on actors who help with any part of an Iranian airline’s flight. “If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel. You cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” he went on.

Bessent boasted that the U.S. has already implemented a host of secondary sanctions on banks that the U.S. accuses of providing support to the Iranian government, including in Egypt, Turkey, and Russia. He suggested that the Trump administration has also been having “behind the scenes discussions” with Chinese authorities, who Bessent said “have been very engaged in the process.”

These sanctions are being done under authorities granted to the president after 9/11, the treasury secretary said, which is “when we were given many of the authorities that we have now.”

The U.S. already imposed sanctions on 27 Iranian airlines earlier this month. Bessent said the sanctions were “a warning to anyone doing business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned today: You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system.”

The measures will further cut off Iranian civilians from traveling abroad. Mahan Air, a top Iranian airline, already said prior to Bessent’s announcement that it was suspending flights to Oman and Turkey. And, as part of its sweeping sanctions regime this month, the U.S. already cut off Iranians from taking tests that allow students to apply to English-language graduate programs across the world.

Meanwhile, economic sanctions are increasingly squeezing Iranian civilians, who are the most severely affected by the wartime sanctions. Many Iranians have lost their jobs as the Iranian economy has shrunk by 10 percent between March 21 and June 20. Prices for regular goods like energy and food have skyrocketed — and, at the same time, the value of the rial has plummeted, making it doubly difficult for families to afford to live.

The sanctions on Iranian airlines may also raise costs to travel out of the country, in effect working to trap Iranian civilians as Trump makes genocidal threats against the entire country and its 92 million inhabitants.

On Sunday, President Donald Trump told Fox News’s Trey Yingst that he is in a “deciding mode” on Iran, and that “very big things” will be happening on the issue soon. Yingst said that Trump “described the current choices on the table as ‘wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal.’”

“My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up?” Trump said, per Yingst. “They better behave.” Such genocidal threats have become commonplace for Trump amid the war.

These comments come as the U.S. has been accused by independent UN officials of committing war crimes against civilians in Iran.

This September, Truthout is celebrating 25 years of publication. For over two decades, we have been a trusted source for fiercely independent journalism thanks to readers like you.

As we look to the next 25 years, we have launched a special fundraising campaign. Looking to a sustainable future for our publication, we have a fundraising goal of $52,000 in the next 72 hours.

We are asking for your support at this juncture because we face greater threats than ever before in our organizational history. Trump and his MAGA allies are determined to control the information ecosystem, and movement-based organizations are subject to dangerous censorship and scrutiny.

If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work and our legacy. Anything you can do makes a difference!

author: Jake Johnson
title: TV Networks Decline Pool Coverage After Trump Bans News Outlets from White House
content:
CNN, MS NOW, and Politico are suing the Trump administration for banning their networks from the White House.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The major U.S. television networks launched what was described as a boycott against TV pool coverage of President Donald Trump on Monday after the White House dropped CNN from the network’s scheduled pool assignment, escalating the administration’s assault on the country’s most prominent media organizations and press freedom.

CNN was set to act as the television pool network accompanying the president during his trip to the United Nations General Assembly this week, but the administration stripped the network of its assignment shortly after Trump banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House, prompting a retaliatory lawsuit from the three outlets.

The major television networks typically rotate responsibility for traveling video coverage of the president. Bryan Boughton, Washington, D.C. bureau chief for Fox News and current chair of the TV press pool, said Monday morning that “effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the president.”

“This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties,” Boughton added. “There will be no replacement pool put in place.”

Scott Nover, a media reporter with The Washington Post, noted that “it’s effectively a boycott by the fellow members — ABC, CBS, NBC, and FOX.”

“There will effectively be no TV coverage of Trump’s UN visit or other presidential events, though I imagine smaller networks may take the White House’s own feed,” Nover wrote on social media. “This is a very big deal and one only possible because of solidarity from the whole pool.”

The TV press pool developments unfolded as CNN, MS NOW, and Politico announced early Monday that they intend to sue the Trump administration for banning them from the White House. The outlets argued that the ban, which Trump announced late last week, endangers press freedom and “the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

CNN, MS NOW and Politico announced the lawsuit in a joint statement, describing the legal action as an effort to “protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.”

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the news organizations said. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom.”

The lawsuit came after journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied access to the White House grounds early Saturday, hours after Trump announced in a social media tirade that he was banning the outlets. Trump, without providing any examples, accused the three outlets of publishing “fiction and lies when they’re covering the president of the United States” — and suggested other news outlets could also be banned in the near future.

When Politico reporter Cheyenne Haslett attempted to enter the White House on Saturday in the wake of Trump’s social media post, Secret Service denied her access and confiscated her press pass. Journalists from the other two outlets reported similar experiences.

“We stand by her and all reporters here covering the White House,” Jonathan Greenberger, Politico’s global editor-in-chief, wrote in response to the incident involving Haslett. “We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights.”

The media outlets’ lawsuit is set to be filed Monday in a federal district court in Washington, D.C. The suit aims to restore the outlets’ White House access and alleges that Trump’s ban violates free press and due process protections.

“The president’s ban of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House is a direct assault on the First Amendment and a blatant violation of due process,” said Ted Boutrous, an attorney for the outlets. “The president has been explicit that this ban is intended to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to intimidate journalists and news organizations covering him and his administration. This ban on the free press harms the American people, who are entitled to rigorous, fact-based coverage of the president of the United States. The law is on our side across the board, and we look forward to presenting our arguments to the court as soon as possible.”

author: Daron Letts
title: Former Iqaluit mayor launches AI-driven site to monitor municipal issues
content:
How many new homes can Iqaluit’s water reservoir support?


Former Iqaluit mayor Kenny Bell is using artificial intelligence program ChatGPT to investigate this question and more, on his newly launched City Hall Record website.


The idea, Bell said, is to track long-term municipal issues that may have fallen by the wayside.


“I’m engaging as a citizen that’s also interested in our community,” Bell said Friday in a phone interview. “It’s really hard to go on the city website and find minutes and listen to records and stuff — especially if you don’t know what you’re looking for.”


Bell was elected to a four-year term as Iqaluit mayor in 2019. He

resigned

 in 2022.


This week, he posted what he calls his first investigation, which charts a timeline of Iqaluit’s water woes through the city’s website, council and committee meetings, and public documents.


The water capacity of the city’s reservoir, Lake Geraldine, was a

major issue

 during his tenure, with many years spent in a state of emergency with

mandatory water conservation efforts

.


He tried to see if ChatGPT could determine how many more homes the existing municipal water infrastructure could service. The program reported it had 13 unanswered questions, which have been sent to City of Iqaluit spokesperson Geoff Byrne.


“No response has been recorded here yet,” the website reported as of Monday.


Nunatsiaq News also asked Byrne

for the number of houses the municipal water system can support.


 “The figure is approximately 3,230 residential units on a population-equivalent basis,” Byrne replied, citing figures from the city’s 2022 general plan.


During his term as city councillor, Bell

often criticized

 the city for a lack of clarity with the public.


“If I as a councillor can’t get information from the city, I can only imagine that citizens that have concerns can’t get information either,” he said back in 2013.


Bell doesn’t self-define as an independent journalist but as a citizen who is interested in sharing information for the benefit of other citizens, including those who work in the media.


“I want to make it easier for people to understand just how hard most issues are [to follow], even for the people that are in the know,” he said, adding ChatGPT simplifies the work.


“It makes it so easy — you ask it a question and it knows everything,” he said.


Acknowledging the fact that artificial intelligence tends to lean into a user’s biases, Bell said he edits the data before it goes online.


Mayor Solomon Awa declined an interview request about the website and Bell’s concerns about transparency.

author: Lillian Kollross
title: Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Have Nearly Doubled: Are Abortion Bans the Cause?
content:
The number of ectopic pregnancy deaths has doubled over the past five years, according to a recent ProPublica analysis of federal data. Almost 200 women have died from ectopic pregnancy between 2020 and 2025. While ectopic pregnancy deaths increased nationwide, the increase was greater in states with strict abortion bans.

An ectopic pregnancy occurs when a fertilized egg implants outside of the uterus, most commonly in the fallopian tubes. The pregnancy cannot develop normally outside of the uterus. If left untreated, the egg will continue to develop until the fallopian tubes rupture, leading to life-threatening internal bleeding.

Ectopic pregnancies are relatively rare, making up about 2% of all pregnancies, they are still the leading cause of death for women in their first trimester. Since hospitals are not required to report ectopic pregnancies, the exact number of cases is difficult to determine.

However, according to maternal health experts, women should not be dying from ectopic pregnancies. “A death related to ectopic pregnancy should really be a never event,” said Dr. Alice Abernathy, a Philadelphia-based OB-GYN.

One treatment for an ectopic pregnancy is when patients receive an injection of the cancer drug methotrexate, which will stop the cells from growing. Methotrexate can be used when the patient is medically stable and the ectopic pregnancy has not ruptured. If the fallopian tubes burst, emergency surgery is generally required.

In abortion-banned states, doctors can face harsh jail time for assisting in the termination of a pregnancy, regardless of how dire the situation is. This has led some doctors to refuse to treat women with ectopic pregnancies. In fact, 61% of OB-GYNs practicing in states where abortion is banned reported concerns about their legal risk when making decisions about patient care.

Diagnosing an ectopic pregnancy can also take time. Doctors typically use an ultrasound and blood tests to determine when a pregnancy is developing. In some cases, the embryo is not visible and doctors must order more blood tests, which can take a few days.

But when it comes to ectopic pregnancies, the longer the treatment is delayed, the greater the risk of tubal rupture and death.

In states where abortion is legal, patients can receive life-saving medical care within a few hours. This should be the case everywhere in the United States. Doctors should not have to choose between saving their patient or spending the rest of their lives in jail. Patients should not have to drive across state lines to receive basic healthcare. Women should not die from ectopic pregnancies.

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Nepal’s Floods Are Putting Women and Girls at Greater Risk
content:
As devastating floods continue to affect communities across Nepal, women and girls are facing increased risks of hunger, violence, exploitation, and displacement.

On August 26, a devastating flash flood struck Nepal, destroying homes, roads, bridges and critical infrastructure across several regions near the Nepal-Tibet border. More than 500 people have been killed, nearly 1,000 remain unaccounted for, and around 10,000 homes have been destroyed. But as the communities respond to the disaster, women and girls are facing additional challenges.

According to UN Women, 157,050 women and girls in the districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot have been affected by the floods. The organization has warned that the disaster is increasing existing risks of violence and exploitation while limiting access to health care and other essential services.

Natural disasters do not affect everyone equally and existing inequalities can become more severe when homes, schools, hospitals and other essential services are destroyed. For women and girls who already face barriers to resources, losing access to these services can put their safety and livelihoods at additional risk. Access to food and water is a particular concern. Flooding has damaged infrastructure and disrupted essential services, leaving survivors facing shortages.

Women often carry a disproportionate share of responsibility for caring for children and other family members. During a disaster, unpaid care work can increase while the resources available to families decrease.

Education is also at risk. In communities already experiencing poverty and instability, disruptions to education can have long-term consequences for girls’ futures. Approximately one in three women across the affected districts are illiterate. Limited literacy can make it more difficult to access relief efforts, complete registration services, or independently apply for assistance. During an emergency, when information about food, shelter, health care and financial assistance can be critical to safety, these barriers become even more significant.

Women are also carrying much of the responsibility for supporting their households. About one-third of households in Nepal’s Bagmati Province are headed by women, making women the primary providers for many families. The floods have destroyed homes, businesses and critical infrastructure, leaving these women responsible for supporting their families while rebuilding their lives with fewer financial resources. The destruction has made it harder for women-led households to access income and recover from the disaster. Humanitarian responses must therefore address the specific needs of women and girls.

UN Women is working with the Nepali government, women’s rights organizations, and humanitarian partners to provide essential services and protection. The organization is also supporting a women-led Community Kitchen initiative designed to provide immediate food assistance while creating opportunities for women’s leadership and livelihoods during the recovery process. UN Women has raised $2 million to support women and girls affected by the floods.

The devastation in Nepal will not disappear when the floodwaters recede. Communities will have to rebuild homes, families, and important infrastructure, but recovery must also address the inequalities that existed before the disaster. Women and girls cannot be treated as an afterthought. They need access to safe shelter, food, clean water, health care and education throughout the recovery process. Nepal’s floods demonstrate that disaster relief is not only about rebuilding, but is about making sure that the people who are most vulnerable are not left even further behind.

author: Lillian Kollross
title: One Louisiana Case Could End Telehealth Abortions for the Whole Country
content:
On September 9, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit in New Orleans heard oral arguments in Louisiana v. U.S. Food and Drug Administration, a case that could restrict access to mifepristone nationwide. Louisiana is challenging changes the FDA made to the drug’s Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) in 2023, which removed the requirement that mifepristone be dispensed in person and allowed the medication to be prescribed through telehealth and sent by mail. Mifepristone has been FDA-approved since 2000 and is safe and effective.

Louisiana argues that the FDA’s changes were unlawful and interfere with the state’s ability to enforce its abortion restrictions. In January, Louisiana’s Attorney General Liz Murrill testified before a Senate committee that the “Biden administration knowingly and intentionally undermined Dobbs” by allowing mifepristone to be mailed to patients in states with abortion restrictions.

Since the fall of Roe, the number of clinician-provided abortions has almost doubled, largely thanks to telehealth.

The case could have consequences far beyond Louisiana. Louisiana is seeking to reinstate the in-person dispensing requirement nationwide, which would prevent patients from receiving mifepristone through telehealth, mail, or retail pharmacies. The Fifth Circuit previously ordered the restrictions back into effect in May, but the U.S. Supreme Court paused that ruling, leaving current access in place while the case continues.

Gabrielle McIntyre, Louisiana’s defense attorney from Alliance Defending Freedom, confirmed that the lawsuit’s goal is to end virtual and mail access to abortion pills for the whole country, even in states where abortion is legal. McIntyre insisted, however, that states where abortion is protected would still be able to enforce their “own regulations regarding abortions.”

During the pandemic, the FDA temporarily allowed medical abortion pills to be prescribed through a telehealth appointment. In 2023, the FDA officially revised its rule to allow medical abortion pills to be prescribed virtually. By 2024, one in four abortions were done via a telehealth appointment.

Telehealth can reduce the time, cost, and logistical barriers associated with traveling to an abortion provider. It can be difficult for patients to get to an abortion provider since the average American lives 86 miles from a reproductive health clinic. For women living in abortion-banned states, telehealth is the only way they can get the care and help they need.

Under the current system, a patient in an abortion-banned state such as Louisiana can receive mifepristone through the mail from a provider in a state with a shield law, like Massachusetts. Shield laws are state-level protections for patients, health care providers, and others involved in reproductive health care who may face legal action from another state. Currently, 23 states and Washington, DC, have some form of shield law.

If the FDA’s 2023 rule is ultimately overturned, patients across the country could once again be required to receive mifepristone in person. This will put the health and safety of women and girls all across the country at risk. This ban will not end abortions, it will only lead to a rise in unsafe ones since people will continue to have abortions, whether or not they are legal.

title: KDP and PUK Peshmerga officially placed under joint ministry
content:
The Peshmerga forces previously under the control of the KDP and PUK, two governing parties in southern Kurdistan (northern Iraq), have been brought together under the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI).


The 80th Unit of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the 70th Unit of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) have been placed under the ministry as the First and Second Regions.


Unification process underway since 2022


In 2022, the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs launched a process to unify the armed forces at the urging of the United States. However, a significant part of the Peshmerga structures remained directly under the control of the two dominant parties, the KDP and PUK. Political disputes between the two parties delayed the unification process for years. With the integration of the 70th and 80th units into the structures of the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs, this part of the reform process has now been completed.


Ceremony announces

the completion of the reorganisation and unification


A ceremony was held on Monday, 21 September 2026, to announce the completion of the reorganisation and unification of the Peshmerga forces.


The ceremony was attended by Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani, Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, Deputy Prime Minister Qubad Talabani, Vice Presidents Sheikh Jaafar Sheikh Mustafa and Mustafa Sayyid Qadir, Minister of Peshmerga Affairs Shorsh Ismail, and General Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, Director of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, alongside senior government officials, security and military commanders, representatives of the Global Coalition, ambassadors and consuls.


The ceremony opened with a minute’s silence in honour of the martyrs of Iraq and Kurdistan.


Minister Ismail: The accomplishment belongs to the entire nation


Peshmerga Affairs Minister Shorsh Ismail then delivered a speech announcing the completion of the unification process, describing it as the outcome of a national effort and a strategic plan that had been pursued for years.


“The process of unifying the Peshmerga has been completed today. I congratulate the people and the Peshmerga on this achievement and this organisational step,” Ismail said. He added that the process was the result of “a national will and a strategic plan—both academic and practical—that began years ago.”


Ismail said the achievement had brought the Peshmerga forces together and enabled reforms within the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs. He described the accomplishment as one belonging to the entire nation.


He also said the unified Peshmerga forces would contribute not only to protecting the Kurdistan Region but also to the security and stability of Iraq as a whole, describing the unification as a “major historic achievement” that had overcome numerous obstacles.


The minister thanked all those who had contributed to and supported the process, including Bafel Jalal Talabani, President of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK). He also expressed gratitude for the support and assistance provided by Coalition forces led by the United States, Germany and France, and called for continued support for the unified Peshmerga forces and Iraq’s stability.


Barzani: Peshmerga forces will serve both the Kurdistan Region and Iraq


In his remarks, KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani described the occasion as a historic day for the Kurdistan Region and the Peshmerga forces, saying that the long-running process had resulted in their unification.


Barzani said the KRG had made completing the unification of the Peshmerga a priority within its government programme. He praised the efforts of Nechirvan Barzani and Qubad Talabani, whom he said had played a major role in finalising the process.


He stressed that the Peshmerga forces are part of Iraq’s defence system and underlined the importance of coordination between the Peshmerga and the Iraqi Army. He also called for Peshmerga personnel to enjoy the same rights as members of the Iraqi Army.


Barzani said the Peshmerga defend peaceful coexistence in the Kurdistan Region and thanked Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi for his continued support for the Region.


For his part, Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani said the Peshmerga forces would serve both the Kurdistan Region and Iraq, stressing that following the unification process, no Peshmerga forces would remain outside the Ministry …

title: Hatimoğulları visits the vigil of earthquake victims’ families: Their voices must be heard
content:
DEM Party Co-Chair Tülay Hatimoğulları visited the vigil held by families of victims of the February 6 earthquakes outside Turkey’s Ministry of Justice in Ankara. For eleven days, the families have been demanding a meeting with ministry officials and accountability for construction contractors, building inspection authorities, and state institutions.


The vigil is organized by the “Families Seeking Justice” platform. Outside the ministry, relatives commemorate those killed in the earthquakes by displaying their photographs. Signs include messages such as: “Why are those responsible for February 6 still free?” and “Those who construct unsafe buildings, remove columns, and allow this to happen must be punished.”


“Lack of oversight killed”


Hatimoğulları first spoke with the families about their experiences and demands. She then criticized the fact that the relatives had been waiting for days for a meeting with the Ministry of Justice. The scale of the suffering they have endured is almost impossible to put into words, the politician said. According to official figures, more than 53,000 people were killed, she said, although the actual number was far higher. She stressed that the disaster should not be viewed solely as the consequence of a natural event.


“Natural disasters do not kill. Buildings constructed in disregard of all regulations kill. Buildings in which steel and cement were cut back for the sake of profit kill,” Hatimoğulları said. She added that inadequate inspections and state failures had worsened the consequences of the earthquake. “Those who profited killed so many people. This is a massacre.”


The families therefore demand not only the criminal prosecution of construction contractors. They say those who caused or permitted deficiencies or failed to fulfill their oversight responsibilities must also be held accountable. “The proceedings must not end in impunity but must have consequences so that this suffering is not repeated,” Hatimoğulları said. She said it has long been demonstrated internationally that the impact of major earthquakes can be significantly reduced through earthquake-resistant construction and effective inspections.


“So that others do not have to experience the same”


Hatimoğulları said the families knew that no court ruling could bring back their children, parents, or other relatives. “Their struggle for justice is therefore also focused on the future: They say: No one else should have to go through what we have experienced.” Hatimoğulları described the solidarity among people who had lost relatives in different disasters as an expression of social responsibility. She referred to a mother who lost six relatives in a flood in Kırklareli and joined the vigil in Ankara to demand justice alongside the earthquake victims’ families.


Hatimoğulları also appealed to the police not to make the vigil more difficult. She stressed that the families should not be denied sleeping mats or camping chairs given the cold weather in Ankara. Many police officers, she added, also lost relatives in the earthquakes. “These families are not harming anyone. On the contrary, they are raising public awareness and reminding society of its responsibilities,” Hatimoğulları said.


Call for concrete action


The DEM Party co-chair called on the justice minister and judicial authorities to take concrete steps. She noted that teports documenting failures, criminal complaints, and extensive case files had already been submitted to the courts. “The families are seeking more than simply a meeting at the ministry. After this meeting, they want an assurance that justice will actually be served. The voices and demands of the families must be heard and answered with concrete measures,” she said.


Hatimoğulları was particularly critical of a system of impunity that, she said, benefited those with economic and political influence: “To this day, wealthy and influential people and construction contractors have been protected. Those responsible for building complexes such as the Rönesans Residence, which collapsed in the earthquake, have also been protected. Do not protect them. Those responsible must face the necessary criminal consequences.”


Hatimoğulları thanked the families for keeping the memory of the disaster and the demand for accountability alive. “You are doing this because you are defending the right to life and because you do not want anyone else to die in the future. Your struggle is our struggle.” …

author: Frida Garza
title: Congress Has Not Passed a Farm Bill Since 2018. This Year May Be No Different.
content:
Democrats in the Senate Agriculture Committee have refused to support a farm bill that doesn’t restore SNAP funding.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Last Tuesday, Senator Mitch McConnell returned to Congress after a three-month absence and promptly cast a deciding vote in the Republican-led Agriculture Committee. Back in August, Democrats on the committee blocked the Senate’s version of the farm bill from progressing to a full vote.

But even after McConnell’s vote, the way things are going, it’s unlikely that Congress will pass a farm bill this year, which would mark the fourth straight year that lawmakers have failed to renew the nation’s cornerstone of agricultural policy.

The issues that made Democrats oppose the farm bill last month are still there, meaning the path to surviving a vote on the Senate floor remains unclear. With 53 seats, Republicans hold a majority in the chamber, but they need 60 votes to pass a bill — so they would need to sway several Democrats to their side in a relatively short amount of time. Midterms, after all, are in November.

Democrats mainly oppose the current draft of the bill because it doesn’t reverse cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. Changes to SNAP are typically implemented through the farm bill, which historically was passed every five or so years. However, last summer, President Donald Trump signed into law the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which slashed funding for SNAP by $186 billion.

Democrats in the Senate Agriculture Committee have refused to support a farm bill that doesn’t restore SNAP funding; they have also pushed for a delay in a crucial change to SNAP that would increase states’ administrative costs for running the food assistance program. Since the farm bill that advanced out of committee does neither of these things, it remains difficult to see how Senate Democrats would support this package in a floor vote.

The cuts to SNAP have wide-reaching impacts for millions of low-income families and individuals across the country who rely on it to buy groceries. But it also has implications for the farmers whose customer base includes SNAP benefit users. “The farmers in our network live in rural areas,” said Jody Osmund, a founding member of the FACE Ag Network, a coalition of pasture-based livestock producers. Rural areas, Osmund continued, “have a higher uptake of SNAP participation than urban areas. So it’s hurting our community.”

Because the Senate farm bill also doesn’t delay a change to the cost-sharing structure of SNAP, states could end up with less funding overall for their own agricultural programs. “States are going to have to rethink their budgets,” said Mike Lavender, policy director of the National Sustainable Agriculture Coalition. “That could mean that states are looking at, ‘Hey, do we fund education at this level or do we fund SNAP? Or do we fund transportation or SNAP?’ So this is forcing really difficult decisions that could impact departments of agriculture at the state level.”

These kinds of decisions will hit small- and medium-sized farmers much more than large corporate farms, making the financial calculus of growing food even harder at a time of rising input costs and unstable trade markets.

There is one bright spot in the latest Senate farm bill for many farm groups, and that’s the exclusion of the Save Our Bacon Act, a provision that would have made it easier for livestock producers to employ some of the least humane practices for caging and confining animals on their farms. “It’s encouraging,” said Osmund.

He and other coalition members flew to Washington, D.C., ahead of the Senate committee vote and met with lawmakers in hopes of convincing them to oppose the Save Our Bacon Act. Other pieces of the Senate farm bill that are unpopular with certain agricultural groups include cuts to conservation programs like the Environmental Quality Incentives Program as well as the Conservation Stewardship Program. Yet Osmund argues that these conservation programs don’t just suffer from a lack of adequate funding; they need to be redesigned in order to direct the most amount of money possible to the most sustainable farming practices. He’d like to see fewer conservation dollars going toward, for example, managing animal waste on industrial livestock operations and more money going toward climate adaptation on farms.

author: CMI Argentina
title: 20 años sin López: “Silencio, encubrimiento e impunidad”
content:
Este viernes 18 se cumplieron 20 años de la segunda desaparición de Jorge Julio López, albañil, militante peronista, sobreviviente del terrorismo de Estado. López brindó su testimonio el 28 de junio de 2006 en la causa contra el genocida Miguel Osvaldo Etchecolatz, ex director de Investigaciones de la Policía Bonaerense durante la última dictadura. Dos meses y medio después, López desapareció cuando se dirigía al tribunal, el día de los alegatos. Al día siguiente, Etchecolatz y otros catorce represores fueron condenados por delitos cometidos en el centro de detención clandestino de La Cacha.


Fotos: Indymedia Argentina


A 20 años de la segunda desaparición forzada de Jorge Julio López, la Multisectorial La Plata – Berisso – Ensenada convocó a movilizar exigiendo su aparición con vida. “Pasan los gobiernos, continúa la impunidad”, denunciando, enfatizando la responsabilidad del Estado.


Cientos de personas, vecinxs, activistas y organizaciones se concentraron en Plaza Moreno y movilizaron hacia Gobernación. La pregunta sigue vigente: ¿Qué hicieron con Jorge Julio López?


Los medios populares Pulso Noticias, Otro Viento y Radio Futuro montaron una web interactiva

https://juliolopezpresente.com.ar

 con una línea de tiempo con los testimonios, videos, imágenes, noticias, sobre el caso y las historias de lucha, organización de todas las personas, grupos y organizaciones que acompañaron y mantienen vivo el reclamo.


Invitamos a visitarlo.


A continuación, compartimos el documento de la marcha:


A 20 AÑOS DE LA SEGUNDA DESAPARICION DE JORGE JULIO LÓPEZ


A 20 años de la segunda desaparición de Jorge Julio López, continuamos en esta plaza, miles de compañeres, recordándolo, exigiendo justicia y preguntándonos: ¿Dónde está?


A 20 años de la segunda desaparición de Jorge Julio López, seguimos recibiendo el mismo silencio y la misma impunidad como respuesta.


Jorge Julio López fue un militante político, parte de esa maravillosa generación de revolucionarias y revolucionarios que se comprometió con un cambio social de raíz. Nació en 1929 en General Villegas, provincia de Buenos Aires. De joven se vino a La Plata y, durante más de cuarenta años, trabajó como albañil. Se construyó su propia casa en la esquina de 140 y 69, en el barrio de Los Hornos.


Allí mismo participó, desde 1973, de las actividades de la Unidad Básica “Juan Pablo Maestre”, de la JP y Montoneros de La Plata.


El Estado genocida desató una persecución sobre ese grupo militante entre octubre y noviembre de 1976, secuestrando a una docena de personas del mismo barrio y acribillando y quemando la sede de la Unidad Básica. La mayoría de los compañeros militantes de ese espacio permanecen desaparecidos. Julio López fue secuestrado por primera vez de su casa en Los Hornos, en la noche del 27 de octubre de 1976.


López testimonió por primera vez en el Juicio por la Verdad, en julio de 1999. Contó que estuvo desaparecido durante 160 días, hasta que fue legalizado. Después permaneció 812 días detenido a disposición del Poder Ejecutivo Nacional en la Unidad 9 y fue liberado en junio de 1979.


También participó en dos inspecciones oculares realizadas por la Cámara Federal de La Plata en los Centros Clandestinos de Detención, en agosto de 2001, y señaló los lugares de ejecución y exterminio de personas. Pese al paso del tiempo, había detallado todo el horror vivido durante su secuestro en unos cuadernos con textos y dibujos. Allí contaba su paso por los Centros Clandestinos del Destacamento y Pozo de Arana, las Comisarías 5.ª y 8.ª, y su blanqueo como detenido legal en la Unidad 9.


El testimonio mencionaba a decenas de secuestrados a los que pudo reconocer o de cuyos nombres pudo enterarse, así como a más de una docena de represores, entre ellos Garachico, Aguiar, Urcola, Gijena, Basualdo, Orellana, Gómez, Ponce, Guallama y el propio Etchecolatz. Su caso estuvo patrocinado por la querella del espacio Justicia Ya La Plata.


Nilda Eloy, integrante de la Asociación de Ex Detenidos Desaparecidos, recuerda que, antes de ingresar a dar su testimonio en el juicio a Etchecolatz, en julio de 2006, López pidió permiso para hablar de la militancia en Los Hornos y afirmó: “Va por los compañeros”.


Treinta años después de su primer secuestro, en su valiente testimonio de 2006, López contó que Etchecolatz estaba presente en el operativo de su secuestro y que, en la Comisaría 5.ª, había sido parte de las sesiones de tortura.
